headline: Health Dept Gears Up for Tiruvannamalai Karthigai Deepam
content: Chennai: The health department has made elaborate medical and public health arrangements for the Karthigai Deepam festival to be held at the Arunachaleswarar Temple in Tiruvannamalai on Monday and Tuesday. Health Minister KG Arunraj reviewed the arrangements via video conference. As many as 120 special medical camps will operate from November 23 to 25 to cater to the large number of devotees expected to attend the festival. Of these, 63 will be located along the Girivalam (circumambulation) route, 25 on major arterial roads, 26 at temporary bus stands and six along the outer ring road. Each camp will have doctors, nurses, pharmacists and multipurpose health workers working round the clock in shifts. Five special medical camps inside the temple premises will have cardiologists. The department has also deployed 45 emergency 108 ambulances, five emergency medical equipment kits (jump kits), one emergency response centre and one emergency control centre. Medical camps along the Girivalam route will be equipped with emergency treatment facilities and foldable stretchers. Medical teams from 12 neighbouring districts have been mobilised and the camps divided into five zones, each supervised by designated officers. Essential medicines, first-aid equipment and life-saving medical facilities have been kept ready to treat fever, fainting, dehydration, heat-related illness, injuries and other emergencies. The department has also stepped up food safety measures at the festival. As many as 297 annadhanam centres have been identified and organisers have been trained in food safety practices. Twenty designated officers and 27 food safety officers, divided into seven teams, will monitor food distribution. Three mobile food testing laboratories have been arranged to check the quality of food items. Around 570 sanitation workers will be deployed at annadhanam centres. A 24-hour control room will function at the district health office from November 23 to 25 to monitor the medical camps, emergency services and field-level activities. The department will coordinate with the police, district administration, local bodies and other agencies to provide emergency medical assistance.

headline: What COP31 collapse means for India – and the future of climate change policy
content: The Antalya climate talks were meant to close on November 20. They ran on for two more days, which made COP31 the longest climate summit on record, and then ended with nothing agreed on. On Sunday afternoon, Murat Kurum, Türkiye's environment minister and the conference president, told the plenary there was no agreement on the text and that the decisions had, therefore, not been adopted. The European Union, the United Kingdom, Panama and small island states including Tuvalu and the Marshall Islands refused a cover decision that said nothing about moving away from fossil fuels. Earlier in the week, the Arab Group and Russia had rejected drafts for the opposite reason, objecting to any language that named energy sources or set sectoral targets. India's environment minister, Bhupender Yadav, said India regretted the failure and that some of its concerns about the proposed text remained unresolved. The question for Indian policymakers is what the country gained and lost in Antalya, and what it should carry to Addis Ababa, where Ethiopia hosts COP32 next year. The one clear win came on day one India's most concrete gain was procedural, and it came before the substantive talks began. On November 9, during the opening plenary, parties agreed to include the Climate Finance Work Programme as a standalone agenda item. The work programme is a result of last year's Mutirão decision in Belém and relates to the provision of finance under Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement, which refers to finance provision by developed countries. The EU opined that there was no separate item emerging from Belém and sought to conclude the work within its two-year term, while India disagreed and prevailed on this. This may sound trivial, but it is very important. For years, developing countries have been focusing on discussions about how much money is being pledged. The dedicated agenda item allows them to ask about the predictability of resources, the ratio of grants to loans, and whether these resources are going to where they are needed. Yadav also came back to this point in his closing remark: Ambition must be backed by resources. There were also two defeats in the struggle over the agenda. The demand of the African Group for an agenda item on tripling adaptation finance was defeated, much to India's regret. The demand for an agenda item on trade and climate change was also defeated, the EU maintaining that this was best addressed in its existing trade discussions. For India, whose steel and aluminium producers are now under pressure from the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, there is no space in the negotiations for discussions on unilateral trade measures. Adaptation money, deferred again For a nation that spends every summer battling heat waves and every monsoon battling floods, the adaptation result is the biggest failure. UNEP's latest Adaptation Gap Report puts developing countries' needs at about $305 billion a year by 2035. International public finance for adaptation was between $28.2 billion and $31.7 billion in 2024. The presidency’s initial drafts attempted to quantify the Belém pledge to triple adaptation finance by 2035, proposing a concrete figure of at least $120 billion per year, with the Standing Committee on Finance determining the baseline at COP32. By the final draft, this figure had disappeared, leaving only the vague goal of tripling. The entire text then fell. Even $120 billion would only have covered between one-fifth and one-third of the estimates of need. Anyone who has worked on a heat action plan or stormwater planning in Indian cities will know how little international adaptation money reaches a municipal corporation. Antalya did nothing to change that. Why India said no to 35 by 35 Electricity was central to the agenda of the Turkish presidency. The cover text called on countries to increase the share of electricity in final energy use to 35 per cent by 2035 from the current 23 per cent. About 90 countries also signed a separate Global Electrification Pledge, committing to the same goal. India was among those that did not sign. During the negotiations, the Like-Minded Developing Countries (LMDC), which India is a part of, felt that the electrification target and the roadmap for fossil fuel transition, which singled out methane, breached their red lines. Yet, this refusal can be defended on its merits. The promise accounts for electricity’s proportion of energy consumption, with no provision that this electricity originates from clean sources, allowing a nation to easily fulfil this promise by simply electrifying based on coal. Methane is another matter. The bulk of India’s methane emissions come from paddy fields and livestock; global action on these would impinge directly on the living of small farmers. India’s efforts ensured its concerns about food security and the role of livelihoods and cultural practices were accounted for in the language on methane. This was certainly an achievement in negotiations, though it no longer appeared in the text. The optics remain clumsy. India has well over 170 GW of solar installed capacity, and electric motorcycles, rooftop solar, and electric buses are all taking off rapidly. On the substance, India is already progressing along the lines of the pledge. Joining Saudi Arabia and Russia, among others, in opposing a sectoral goal risks marking India as part of a hindering bloc, even if its motivations are very different from those of those countries. India could easily dispel this notion by publishing its own sectoral electrification blueprint and illustrating those domestic goals, rather than a global proportion, define its route to the target. Just transition and the road to Addis Ababa COP31 was also supposed to set up the just transition mechanism agreed in principle at Belém. Talks stalled over where it should sit and who should run it. India argued for a two-tier, country-driven design and repeated that energy transitions must be nationally determined, backed by finance, technology and capacity-building for developing countries. That argument will return at COP32, along with most of what Antalya left open. The seventh review of the financial mechanism had already been pushed to next year. The adaptation finance baseline, the trade question and the shape of the just transition mechanism now travel to Addis Ababa unsettled. India has good reason to prepare early. The finance work programme is now formally on the table, and India will need worked-out proposals on the quality and predictability of finance rather than restatements of Article 9.1. An African presidency is also likely to put adaptation finance at the centre, and on that issue India's interests sit very close to Africa's. A joint push on the adaptation baseline would do more for Indian cities than another round of blocking. There is a larger stake as well. India says it values consensus-based multilateralism, and it offered in 2023 to host COP33. A process that cannot agree on a cover text after two weeks and two days of overtime is a weak platform for that ambition. What Antalya showed is that India can win a procedural argument over finance and still leave without the money its cities and farmers need to adapt. Closing that distance is the work of the next 12 months. The writer is Professor of Public Policy at FLAME University. He has been contributing to various IPCC reports and presently a Lead Author in IPCC’s special report on Climate Change and Cities

headline: Pune & Pimpri-Chinchwad To Witness Auto-Rickshaw Shutdown Over Proposed Bike Taxi Policy
content: Pune: Commuters in Pune and Pimpri-Chinchwad may face inconvenience on Monday as auto-rickshaw unions have called for a shutdown in protest against the Maharashtra government's proposed policy to permit bike taxi services. The Rickshaw Panchayat, along with other driver organisations, will stage demonstrations outside the offices of Minister of State for Transport Madhuri Misal and Maharashtra Legislative Assembly Deputy Speaker Anna Bansode at 11 am, demanding that the government scrap the proposed policy.The demonstrations will be held outside Misal's office in her Parvati constituency and Bansode's office in Pimpri. The unions have demanded a permanent ban on bike taxi services in metropolitan areas, alleging that their introduction would worsen traffic congestion and adversely affect the livelihoods of auto-rickshaw drivers.According to the Rickshaw Panchayat, auto-rickshaws operate under several regulatory requirements, including mandatory insurance, fitness certificates, prescribed fares, vehicle colour codes and driver uniforms. However, private two-wheelers operating as bike taxis would not face equivalent regulatory obligations, creating unfair competition for traditional auto-rickshaw operators.The dispute dates back to 2022, when several auto-rickshaw unions protested outside the Pune Regional Transport Office (RTO) against the government's move to permit bike taxi services. The Rickshaw Panchayat subsequently approached the Bombay High Court and the Supreme Court, challenging the proposal. The courts did not grant permission for bike taxi operations and directed the state government to formulate a policy on the issue.The government later constituted a committee headed by former bureaucrat Ramanath Jha to examine the matter. The Rickshaw Panchayat presented its objections before the committee, which recommended that bike taxis should not be permitted in metropolitan areas and that their operations should be restricted to remote and inaccessible regions.Bad Weather In Patna Forces IndiGo Pune-Patna Flight Carrying 187 Passengers To Divert To LucknowHowever, the government's renewed efforts to introduce bike taxi services have prompted the unions to resume their agitation.Nitin Pawar, president of the Rickshaw Panchayat, said the organisations would approach elected representatives to demand the complete withdrawal of the proposed policy. The Rickshaw Panchayat, Azad Rickshaw Sanghatana and Chhava Vahan Chalak Kamgar Sangh will jointly organise the protest.Auto-rickshaw services in Pune and Pimpri-Chinchwad will remain suspended during the demonstrations on Monday.

headline: Dipika Kakar’s health: Shoaib Ibrahim dismisses reports of another surgery, says ‘please don’t spread false claims’
content: Shoaib Ibrahim, 39, dismissed news claiming his wife, actor Dipika Kakar, is "serious" and set to undergo another surgery. "It's important to talk about this. I saw a news item on a portal misleadingly claiming that Dipika will be undergoing surgery. This is seriously wrong. There is nothing like this. We had an RFA (radiofrequency ablation; a minimally invasive procedure) in February. There's been nothing after that. People get misled, and then messages start coming in. There is no surgery. Things are improving. Please don't spread false claims regarding health. Many people want to see us healthy and happy. In today's times, I understand engagement is necessary, but not when it comes to health. This is our request," he said on his YouTube channel, alongside Dipika. Dipika added, "Looking at such an item, anyone would feel that.oh.there is another surgery happening? Don't do this. This is wrong." Shoaib added, "The journey of recovery is long. Not every month is the same. It will take time. Grateful for your wishes and abide by God's will." DISCLAIMER: This article is based on information from the public domain and/or the experts we spoke to. The emotional damage of health rumours is something we rarely talk about, said Delnna Rrajesh, psychotherapist, relationship breakthrough coach, and founder of Kintsugi Radiance Academy. "For someone navigating a serious illness, an unverified headline is not just misinformation. It can reopen fears, disrupt emotional recovery and force a family to relive something they are already struggling to cope with," she told indianexpress.com. One of the most difficult aspects of living with a serious illness is uncertainty. "Even when treatment is progressing, patients may remain emotionally sensitive to anything suggesting another setback. A routine appointment, an unexpected symptom or an upcoming medical report can bring back fears they thought they had started managing. I see how challenging it can be for individuals and families to rebuild their sense of emotional security after a frightening experience. The mind can become particularly alert to anything that resembles the original threat. A misleading report about another surgery can therefore carry far more emotional weight than the person sharing it realises. It may bring back memories of hospitalisation, physical discomfort, difficult conversations and the fear of what lies ahead," shared Delnna. This does not mean every patient will react in the same way. But it is precisely why health-related information deserves greater sensitivity and accuracy. "When inaccurate health news spreads, the affected person and their family often become responsible for correcting it. Imagine receiving twenty messages asking whether your condition has worsened. Each message may come from genuine love and concern. But answering the same frightening question repeatedly can become emotionally exhausting. I often encourage families to understand the difference between expressing concern and unintentionally transferring anxiety to someone who is already vulnerable," said Delnna. Shoaib's observation that every month is different also highlights something important about the emotional experience of recovery. "We tend to view healing as a steady progression from illness to wellness. But recovery from serious medical conditions can involve periods of improvement, difficult days, treatment-related discomfort and continuing uncertainty. Psychologically, this unpredictability can be challenging. A person may feel hopeful one day and overwhelmed the next. They may feel grateful for their progress while also worrying about future medical results. These emotions can coexist without indicating a lack of strength or positivity," described Delnna. Public figures may choose to share parts of their health journeys, and their openness can help others feel less alone. But sharing personal experiences does not mean surrendering the right to privacy. "For someone navigating illness, deciding what to share, when to share it and whom to tell can provide a valuable sense of personal control. Unverified reporting can take that control away. This is not simply about celebrities. Even within families, repeatedly discussing someone's diagnosis, forwarding medical reports or asking intrusive questions without permission can leave the individual feeling exposed. Concern does not automatically give us access to another person's medical information," stressed Delnna. DISCLAIMER: This article is based on information from the public domain and/or the experts we spoke to.

headline: BJP Unveils ‘Triple S’ Formula For Uttar Pradesh 2027
content: Lucknow: With the 2027 UP Assembly elections approaching, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) is intensifying preparations to retain power for a third consecutive term. The party’s electoral strategy is expected to revolve around law and order, women’s safety, welfare schemes, infrastructure development, religious issues and strengthening its organisational machinery.SP-Congress Seat-Sharing Talks To Begin For UP 2027 Polls, Congress Stakes Claim To 181 Seats The BJP is planning to reinforce coordination between the government, party organisation and alliance partners under its “Triple S” formula—Sangathan (organisation), Sarkar (government) and Sahyogi Dal (allies). The approach aims to improve coordination, strengthen grassroots engagement and ensure that government achievements reach voters effectively.Amethi Prayer Meet Sparks Conversion Row; Several Detained Beneficiary outreach is expected to remain a major component of the campaign. The party plans to connect directly with people benefiting from welfare schemes, including women, farmers, economically weaker sections and youth. Voter-list management, booth-level strengthening and digital monitoring are also likely to receive priority.Women’s safety and empowerment are expected to feature prominently in the BJP’s campaign narrative. Schemes such as Mukhyamantri Kanya Sumangala Yojana, widow pensions, Safe City initiatives and proposed welfare programmes for women are likely to be highlighted as part of the government’s achievements.UP Govt Plans New Teaching Duties For Teachers Assigned Census & Election Work, B.Ed & BTC Trainees To Benefit The party is also expected to focus on youth through employment-oriented initiatives, skill development, educational support, free coaching programmes and entrepreneurship opportunities.Infrastructure and development projects, including expressways, industrial corridors, Jewar airport, investment initiatives and religious tourism projects in Ayodhya, Varanasi and Mathura-Vrindavan, will form another important pillar of the campaign.Alongside governance and development, the BJP is likely to sharpen its ideological messaging around Hindutva, Ram Mandir, Krishna Janmabhoomi and the Uniform Civil Code (UCC). These issues could play a significant role in mobilising its core voter base.The emerging strategy suggests that the BJP will combine welfare delivery, development, women-centric initiatives, organisational strength and cultural nationalism to shape its campaign for the 2027 electoral battle.

headline: 5-bed ICUs in taluk hospitals, IVF centres for women in Karnataka
content: KALABURAGI The government of Karnataka is planning to establish intensive care units (ICUs) with a minimum capacity of five beds in every taluk hospital, introduce telemedicine services, and set up government-run in-vitro fertilisation (IVF) centres for women, Health and Family Welfare Minister U.T. Khader said on November 22. Addressing a press conference in Bidar, Mr. Khader said the government was taking steps to strengthen the public healthcare system and provide quality medical services to people, particularly in rural areas. ‘Facilities provided to government school students in Karnataka must be better than those in private schools’ ‘Facilities provided to government school students in Karnataka must be better than those in private schools’ Health Minister U.T. Khader directs officials to reject substandard uniforms, bags and footwear; calls for better hostel facilities and school infrastructure ‘Facilities provided to government school students in Karnataka must be better than those in private schools’ storyline 1 The proposed five-bed ICUs in taluk hospitals would help provide initial treatment to patients suffering from serious ailments at the taluk level. Telemedicine facilities would be developed to enable people in rural areas to access medical advice and treatment without having to travel to district hospitals, he added. “The government has initiated the recruitment process for more than 200 MBBS doctors and had approved the appointment of around 1,000 healthcare personnel, including doctors and nurses. Recruitment of doctors, nurses, laboratory technicians and pharmacists would be taken up to address staff shortages in primary health centres,” he said. QR codes for food and drug safety The Minister said that the government was introducing a QR code-based complaint mechanism in hotels, shops and medical stores to lodge complaints about substandard food, counterfeit medicine, denial of bill, and other quality-related violations. “Officials concerned would immediately visit the establishment and take appropriate action on receiving a complaint. To strengthen the Food Safety Department, the Chief Minister has approved the recruitment of another 25 officers in addition to the existing 25,” he said. Government IVF centres in four cities Mr. Khader said that the government was formulating a separate women’s health programme to address health issues affecting women at different stages of life. Pointing out that fertility treatment in private hospitals often involved expenditure running into lakhs of rupees, Mr. Khader said that the government has planned to establish IVF centres in major urban centres. Health Department to soon launch Ruthu Thare, a State-wide campaign to deal with perimenopause and menopause storyline 1 “Government-run IVF centres will be established in Mangaluru, Bengaluru, Mysuru and Kalaburagi in the first phase. They would provide relief to women from poor and middle-income families,” he said. 350 new ambulances The government had provided 350 new ambulances to improve emergency healthcare services. With 450 ambulances already in operation, the addition of the new vehicles would take the total fleet to around 800, enabling timely emergency services across Karnataka, he said. Assurance to ASHA workers Responding to a question on the demands of ASHA workers for an increase in their honorarium, the Minister appealed to them to call off their protest and give the government time to address their concerns. Karnataka Chief Minister assures ASHA workers of decision on their demands after Winter Session storyline 1 ASHAs reject government’s assurance; decide to continue protest storyline 1 He said the Chief Minister had discussed the issue for nearly an hour and had assured that the matter would be taken up with Cabinet colleagues and officials after the winter session of the legislature. A decision on increasing the honorarium could not be taken overnight and requires consultation, he said. Explaining the existing payment structure, Mr. Khader said the Centre provides ₹2,000, while the State Government contributes ₹5,000, besides an incentive of ₹1,000, taking the total monthly payment to ₹8,000. ASHA workers are seeking an increase to ₹15,000 a month, he said. The government had also written to the Union Health Minister and the Prime Minister regarding their demands. He urged the workers to place their trust in the government of Karnataka and allow some time to respond, adding that they could resume their protest if their demands were not addressed after the Assembly session.

headline: A Kentucky health-care fraud defendant owing $3.77 million in restitution tried to stop the $2.4 million
content: A Kentucky man's attempt to prevent the sale of a commercial property linked to his health-care fraud case has been rejected by a federal appeals court. Timothy Ehn, who owes more than $3.77 million in court-ordered restitution, wanted to stop a $2.4 million transaction involving a building owned by a company in which he previously held a 50% stake.The US Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit dismissed three appeals filed by Ehn on Friday. According to the ruling, judges found that he had missed the deadline for challenging the sale approval. They also ruled that his subsequent bankruptcy filing had affected his legal right to contest decisions involving the company's assets.The property, located at 8780 US 42 in Florence, Kentucky, belongs to GT Enterprise LLC. It was the company's primary asset and had been put up for sale during efforts to recover money owed by Ehn and another defendant, William Siefert.The sale was approved by a federal district court on September 16 for $2.4 million. The transaction was scheduled to close on November 23. Ehn approached the appeals court seeking to prevent the deal from going ahead while his legal challenges remained unresolved.How property came under court-appointed receiverThe dispute traces back to a health-care fraud case in which a jury found Ehn and Siefert guilty. Their sentences included financial restitution orders. Ehn was directed to pay $3,773,569.30, while Siefert was ordered to pay $1,968,763.10.The government subsequently sought to recover these amounts by placing liens on the defendants' ownership interests in GT Enterprise. Both men owned half of the company.The district court approved the government's request and appointed Michael B Baker to oversee GT Enterprise and its assets. The receiver was given responsibility for handling the company's property and was allowed to arrange its sale, provided the court approved the transaction.The receiver later approached the district court with a proposal to sell the Florence property for $2.4 million. The court accepted the proposal on September 16.Ehn objected to the steps taken during the receivership proceedings. Once the sale received court approval, he sought to prevent the money generated by the transaction from being distributed. He also wanted the transfer of ownership and other steps connected with the deal stopped.The district court refused to grant his request. Ehn then took the dispute to the Sixth Circuit, asking it to intervene before the scheduled closing.Why appeals court rejected his first challengeOne of Ehn's challenges concerned the district court's decision to approve the sale. However, the appeals court found that he had waited too long to formally contest that order.The applicable deadline in a criminal case is 14 days from the date of the order being challenged. Since the property sale received approval on September 16, Ehn needed to file his appeal within that period. His formal notice of appeal was filed only on November 9.Ehn argued that a motion he had submitted on September 21 should count as an earlier notice of appeal. That application had sought replacement legal representation, more time and protection of the receivership's records and assets.The judges did not accept this argument. They found that the September application did not clearly identify the decision being challenged or specify the court where the appeal was intended to be heard. It therefore did not meet the requirements for a valid notice of appeal.Ehn also disputed the use of the 14-day deadline. He argued that since the government was recovering restitution through a civil process, the longer 60-day appeal period should apply.The court rejected this distinction. It said the underlying case remained criminal, making the 14-day deadline applicable. His November filing was consequently too late for the court to consider his challenge to the sale approval.Bankruptcy left Ehn without right to second appealThe timing of Ehn's bankruptcy filing created a separate problem for his attempt to stop the transaction. He had filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy on September 16, the same day the district court approved the sale. In his bankruptcy proceedings, he listed his 50% ownership interest in GT Enterprise among his assets.The appeals court explained that this interest became part of his bankruptcy estate when he filed the petition. Under Chapter 7 proceedings, a trustee takes control of the debtor's non-exempt assets and handles matters concerning the estate.This meant Ehn could no longer independently pursue claims relating to his former ownership interest in GT Enterprise. The bankruptcy trustee was the person legally entitled to take action on matters affecting that interest.The trustee, however, had not appealed the district court's refusal to halt the property sale. Ehn could not file an appeal using the trustee's rights, the judges said.Ehn had also argued that the commercial property itself did not belong to his bankruptcy estate. The court said this did not resolve the issue because the relevant asset was his stake in GT Enterprise.That ownership interest had already become part of the bankruptcy estate. The court therefore found that Ehn could not demonstrate the legal standing required to challenge the order refusing to stop the sale.Court dismisses all three appealsThe Sixth Circuit concluded that it could not hear Ehn's challenges. His appeal against the sale approval was filed outside the permitted period, while his challenge to the refusal to halt the transaction failed because he no longer had the necessary legal standing.The court also dismissed a separate appeal concerning the district court's refusal to allow additional material and appoint legal counsel. It found that this decision was not among the types of orders that could be appealed at that stage.With all three appeals dismissed, Ehn's emergency request to suspend the property sale no longer had a pending appeal to support it. The judges therefore rejected that request as moot.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

headline: ‘I ate two eggs every day for a month’: The impact on my cholesterol levels
content: Eggs are an excellent source of protein and several essential nutrients, but their cholesterol content often raises questions about how often to eat them. While some people enjoy eggs as part of their daily diet, others worry that eating them regularly could affect their blood cholesterol levels. So, what happens when you eat two eggs every day for a month? We examine the available evidence and ask nutrition experts what you should know. Does eating two eggs every day raise cholesterol levels? Dt Deepali Sharma, clinical nutritionist at the CK Birla Hospital®, Delhi, says, "Eating two eggs every day for a month does not necessarily lead to a significant rise in cholesterol levels. While eggs are a source of dietary cholesterol, their impact on blood cholesterol varies from one person to another and depends on overall dietary patterns, genetics, and metabolic health." DISCLAIMER: This article is based on information from the public domain and/or the experts we spoke to. Always consult your health practitioner before starting any routine. "Two large eggs contain approximately 370–400 mg of dietary cholesterol, primarily concentrated in the yolks. However, dietary cholesterol does not translate directly into an equivalent increase in blood cholesterol. The liver regulates cholesterol production, and in most healthy individuals, it compensates to some extent for the cholesterol consumed through food," she adds. What research suggests Research suggests that egg consumption may modestly increase total, LDL, and HDL cholesterol in some people, although the effect varies by individual and depends on the overall diet, particularly saturated-fat intake. "The overall effect on the LDL-to-HDL ratio varies. Some people, particularly those who are genetically predisposed or have underlying metabolic conditions, may experience a more pronounced rise in LDL cholesterol," Dt Sharma explains. The pairings matter Stressing that it is equally important to consider what accompanies the eggs, Dt Sharma says, "Consuming eggs with butter, processed meats, sausages or high-fat cheese can increase saturated fat intake, which has a more established association with elevated LDL cholesterol. While pairing eggs with vegetables, whole grains and fibre-rich foods makes for a more heart-friendly meal." For most healthy adults, moderate egg consumption can be part of a balanced diet. However, individuals with high LDL cholesterol, familial hypercholesterolaemia, diabetes or established cardiovascular disease should discuss their dietary intake with a healthcare professional. If you have been eating two eggs daily for a month and want to understand their impact, Dt Sharma suggests that a lipid profile can help assess changes in total cholesterol, LDL, HDL and triglycerides. "It must, ideally, be compared with a previous baseline test, while accounting for other dietary and lifestyle changes." 'Eggs' has been trending on Google for the past 24 hours. DISCLAIMER: This article is based on information from the public domain and/or the experts we spoke to. Always consult your health practitioner before starting any routine.

headline: Reimagining India’s higher education ecosystem | Hindustan Times
content: A differentiated ecosystem spanning research, teaching and applied skills can help convert the demographic dividend into a national capability. India’s opportunity lies not merely in expanding higher education, but in organising it more effectively.India’s central higher education question is not whether every institution can become a global research university, but whether institutions can pursue distinct missions and be supported and assessed accordingly. This matters because the demographic dividend is an opportunity, not an inherent natural advantage: A young population becomes a national asset only when its members can access knowledge, acquire relevant capabilities and advance within a changing economy. The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 provides a significant foundation. Its emphasis on multidisciplinary learning, the Academic Bank of Credits and multiple entry and exit points acknowledges the diversity of learner journeys. Realising this ambition also requires a clearer understanding of the distinct roles that institutions can play.A differentiated model may be organised around three complementary missions: research-led universities, teaching-focused universities, and vocational and applied-skills institutions. These do not represent rungs on a ladder of prestige; they are mere distinct means of creating public value.Research-led universities must place high-quality research, consulting, innovation and knowledge creation as their raison d’être. Their work should encompass basic and applied sciences, humanities and interdisciplinary inquiry, technology development, industry collaboration and incubation. This demands specialised faculty, well-equipped laboratories, sustained funding and an environment that supports discovery at the undergraduate, postgraduate, doctoral and post-doctoral levels.Research-led missions require a substantial resource commitment, as established research systems illustrate. In FY2024, US higher education institutions recorded approximately $ 118 billion in research and development expenditure, with the federal government accounting for 55% of academic R&D funding. In the same year, MIT reported approximately $ 2.1 billion in sponsored research expenditure. These figures illustrate the scale of investment behind research-intensive institutions; they are not funding targets for India.Teaching-focused universities have an equally consequential mission: to deliver outstanding learning and to develop an adaptable workforce. Their priorities should include academic quality, strong foundations, relevant programmes, effective pedagogy, student support, industry engagement, placements and lifelong learning. Their success should be measured by what learners know and can do, and by how effectively they progress into employment or further study.Vocational and applied-skills institutions connect learning directly with work. They should offer practical programmes, short courses and qualifications shaped by local and sectoral demand, with curricula that evolve in step with employers, technologies and regional economies. India’s Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs) and polytechnics provide a base on which to build, through stronger industry partnerships, modular learning and progression routes into higher education. These need to be embedded in society and response rapidly as the business requirements change. Countries have developed varied institutional arrangements. The US combines research-intensive universities with teaching-oriented institutions and community colleges. The UK maintains research-intensive universities alongside broad-based and professionally oriented institutions. Germany links universities, universities of applied sciences and vocational training. France has universities as well as the Grandes Écoles and technical pathways.The principal worth adopting is that institutional purpose should shape institutional design.A persistent challenge arises when every institution is encouraged to pursue every ambition. Research requires specialist talent, laboratories, funding and long gestation periods. Teaching excellence requires sustained investment in faculty, pedagogy and student support. Applied-skills education requires strong employer relationships, practical training and frequent curriculum renewal. When institutions distribute limited resources across incompatible priorities, both clarity and quality may suffer.The answer lies not in lowering aspirations but in aligning them: common expectations of integrity and quality can co-exist with assessment against each institution’s declared purpose. Leadership, faculty capabilities, infrastructure, funding and student expectations should reinforce that purpose. Accreditation and ranking frameworks, including NAAC and NIRF, can recognise the different outcomes each mission seeks. A research-led institution should demonstrate research quality and influence; a teaching-focused institution should evidence learning and graduate outcomes; and an applied-skills institution should show employer relevance and how effectively learners’ skills translate into work.Such alignment gives students and families greater clarity about what an institution is designed to do, what outcomes it can credibly promise, and how those outcomes will be measured.India already possesses extraordinary institutional scale. The All-India Survey on Higher Education (AISHE) 2023–24 recorded 1,289 universities or university-level institutions and 48,246 colleges. The task now is to convert this breadth into depth: stronger research where research is the mission, better learning where teaching is the mission, and effective pathways into work where applied skills are the priority.India has demonstrated its capacity to leapfrog in digital public infrastructure, telecommunications and payments. A similar ambition is achievable in higher education, not by asking every institution to do everything, but by enabling each to do its chosen work exceptionally well. Artificial Intelligence (AI) can accelerate discovery, personalise learning and widen access to skills.The opportunity is to create a coherent ecosystem that serves learners, employers, communities and the nation, while welcoming students from across the world. If India aligns institutional missions with investment, talent and meaningful measures of success, it can convert scale into strength and its demographic dividend into lasting capability. The ambition should be for India to become not only one of the world’s largest higher education systems, but also one of its most trusted and sought-after education destinations.(The views expressed are personal)This article is authored by Akshay Munjal, founder, Hero Education & pro-chancellor, BML Munjal University (BMU).

headline: India flash composite PMI rises to 56.3 in November; manufacturing gains
content: India’s private sector activity remained robust in November, with the HSBC Flash India Composite Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) edging up to 56.3 from 56.2 in October, according to data released on Monday. The improvement was driven by faster growth in manufacturing output, which offset a softer expansion in services activity. The HSBC Flash India Manufacturing PMI rose to a nine-month high of 56.0 in November from 54.7 in October. The manufacturing PMI output index increased to 58.3 from 57.0, while the services business activity index eased to 55.3 from 55.8 in October. A reading above 50 indicates expansion from the previous month, while a reading below 50 signals contraction. Total new business increased at the fastest pace since June, supported by stronger demand among manufacturers, while the pace of demand growth in services was unchanged. Survey participants attributed higher sales to favourable market demand and new customer wins. Foreign demand also strengthened, with new export orders rising at the fastest pace in four months. Goods producers continued to record stronger growth in international sales, although the pace eased, while export growth accelerated among service providers.Manufacturing hiring strengthensPrivate sector employment increased marginally in November. Manufacturers added staff at the fastest rate in seven months, while service providers reduced employment for the first time in close to a year, although the decline was marginal. Outstanding business declined for the second consecutive month, reflecting lower incomplete work in the services sector, while manufacturers reported a marginal increase in backlogs. Cost pressures remained subdued during the month, with operating expenses rising only slightly across manufacturing and services. Selling price inflation accelerated from October but remained modest compared with its historical trend. Manufacturers and service providers raised prices at the same pace. “Manufacturing activity gathered momentum, with output and new orders accelerating. The increase in new orders was driven by stronger domestic demand, while new export orders moderated a bit,” said Pranjul Bhandari, chief India economist at HSBC. She added that services saw a softer performance despite a sharp increase in new export business, while input-cost inflation remained subdued and output-price inflation rose modestly.Business confidence improvesBusiness sentiment strengthened in November, with overall confidence regarding activity over the coming year rising to its highest level since May. However, the index remained below its long-run average. Optimism improved among both manufacturers and service providers. Manufacturers also increased input purchases at the fastest pace since May, while stocks of purchases rose at the quickest rate in nine months. Holdings of finished goods increased by the greatest extent since the survey began in March 2005.

headline: PM Modi to unveil development projects worth Rs 34,470 crore in Bihar on November 21
content: 21/11/26 | 9:34 am | Bihar | Narendra Modi | PM Modi | Prime Minister Prime Minister Narendra Modi will visit Bihar on November 21, to inaugurate, dedicate to the nation and lay the foundation stones of development projects worth around ₹34,470 crore in Vaishali. The projects cover road connectivity, energy, urban infrastructure, water resources, education, healthcare, transport and other key sectors. The Prime Minister will visit Nitish Setu in Vaishali district at around 1:15 PM. At approximately 2 PM, he will inaugurate and dedicate various projects to the nation, lay the foundation stones for several new initiatives and address a public gathering. The projects are aimed at strengthening infrastructure, improving public services and supporting economic development across Bihar. Nitish Setu to Strengthen Connectivity Between North and South Bihar A major highlight of the visit will be the dedication of Nitish Setu, an extradosed cable-stayed bridge over the River Ganga, to the nation. Built at an estimated cost of ₹4,280 crore, the 19.7-km-long project connects Kachhi Dargah on NH-22 in Patna district with Bidupur on NH-322 in Vaishali district.

headline: Weekly policy watch: Nepal PM Shah's India visit, PMI flash data in focus
content: India’s diplomatic and economic calendar this week will focus on Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s visit to New Delhi, along with fresh readings on manufacturing and services activity. Nepal PM Balendra Shah to hold talks with Modi Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah is scheduled to hold delegation-level talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday. The two leaders are expected to review the full range of India-Nepal relations and exchange views on regional and international issues of mutual interest, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said. Shah arrived in India on Sunday for a two-day state visit from November 22 to 23 at PM Modi’s invitation. This is his first visit to India since taking office in March 2026 and his first bilateral visit abroad as Nepal’s prime minister. External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar met Shah in New Delhi on Sunday and said India values its special friendship with Nepal. In a post on X, Jaishankar shared a photograph of the meeting and said he looked forward to Shah’s engagements with PM Modi on Monday. PMI Flash data on November 23 The HSBC Manufacturing and Services PMI Flash data for November will be released on November 23. India’s manufacturing activity moderated in October, with the HSBC India Manufacturing PMI falling to 54.7 from 55.1 in September. Growth in output and new orders slowed during the month. However, strong overseas demand pushed new export orders to a six-month high, while selling price inflation fell to its lowest level in nearly four years. The services sector, meanwhile, expanded at its fastest pace in four months in October, supported by stronger domestic demand and new business orders. The HSBC India Services PMI rose to 55.8 in October from 55.2 in September, marking the strongest expansion since June. The reading remained above the 50 mark, which separates expansion from contraction, as well as its long-term average. New business increased at its fastest pace in four months, with companies citing favourable demand, new client acquisitions and successful advertising campaigns. Deposit growth data on November 27 The RBI will release bank deposit growth data on November 27, offering an update on the pace at which banks are attracting deposits. Deposit growth in India rose to 16.9 per cent in the week ended October 30 from 16.7 per cent two weeks earlier. Deposit growth averaged 14.72 per cent between 1998 and 2026. It reached a record high of 29.3 per cent in January 2008 and a low of 2.7 per cent in December 2017. Forex reserves data on November 27 The RBI will release foreign exchange reserves data for the week ended November 20 on November 27. India’s forex reserves fell by $14.21 billion to $705.34 billion in the week ended November 13, according to the latest RBI data. Reserves had stood at $719.55 billion in the previous week ended November 6. Foreign currency assets (FCAs), the largest component of the reserves, declined by $7.9 billion to $583.45 billion during the reported week.

headline: A thriving economy and Rahul Gandhi fuming with jealousy
content: Why do universities in a super-rich and developed country like the United States (even though the bubble of this superpower has begun to burst) invite Rahul Gandhi to deliver lectures? It’s a question even Vikramaditya would not be able to answer if Vetal asks him! India is blessed with a large number of scholars across the fields of politics, economics, culture, religion, science and technology. Many among them present their views in a balanced and unbiased manner.Despite this, why renowned universities in the United States invite Rahul Gandhi, who is miles away from knowledge and intellectual depth, to deliver speeches remains a mystery. But if they also share the same mindset, then the case is closed! Anyway, the point was about the statement made by Yuvraj Rahul Gandhi at Columbia University in the United States. He said that India is sitting on an economic disaster. He also mocked the Modi government's initiatives, such as Make in India and Startup. He did not share any details about why the Indian economy is in a bad state. He does not have the ability to thoroughly analyse the state of the economy.Therefore, it is not even expected of him. It is unlikely that he is even aware of the criteria used to determine whether an economy is strong or weak. Such questions are never directed at him. Nobody in the United States countered him by asking how he could make such adverse comments about the Indian economy when the International Monetary Fund is projecting India's economic growth at 7%. It's a different matter altogether if universities like Columbia have made specific arrangements to ensure that no counter-questions are raised.American scholars will not ask Rahul Gandhi why a superpower like the United States lifted restrictions on oil purchases from a country whose economy is in such a poor state according to him. It is extremely significant that India is achieving an economic growth rate of 7% despite the war-like situation in West Asia and the challenges posed to oil transportation through the Strait of Hormuz. Anyway. 18 days before Rahul Gandhi's speech, the details of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) collections for October 2026 were released.India's GST collections reached Rs 2.31 lakh crore in October 2026. Compared to October 2025, GST collections grew by 23%, which is the fastest growth in the last four years. October has recorded the highest collection since April in the current financial year 2026–27. In April, the collection was Rs 2.43 lakh crore. Just a year ago, in September 2025, the Modi government while announcing a reduction in GST rates declared that there would be only two slabs, i.e., 5% and 18%, across the country. GST on a few things like bread, paneer and processed milk was reduced to 0% while on other things like soap, toothpaste, shampoo and other everyday items it has been reduced from 18% to 5%. The GST on two-wheelers, three-wheelers, buses, trucks, ambulances, auto parts and cement has been reduced from 28% to 18%. Despite these rate cuts, India's GST collection has recorded a continuous increase over the past one year.While Rahul Gandhi was talking gibberish about the Indian economy in the United States, the details of the performance of India's public sector banks during the first half of the financial year 2026–27 were released. Public sector banks recorded a combined net profit of Rs. 1.10 lakh crore during the first half of the financial year 2026–27 (April to September 2026). Public sector banks in India had become hubs for the distribution of government freebies during Congress rule. These banks had to distribute loans like freebies due to government interference. The Modi government has brought about substantial changes in the working of public sector banks since it came to power in 2014. Its effects are now beginning to show. In a historic performance, public sector banks have collectively recorded a net profit of Rs. 1,09,540 crore during the first six months of the financial year 2026–27. This profit has increased by a whopping 16.9% compared to the same period last year. The business of public sector banks has reached Rs 301.6 lakh crore. There has been a substantial increase of 15.5% in it compared to last year. Non-performing assets (NPAs) of banks are crucial as far as the financial health of these banks is concerned. A non-performing loan is a loan that becomes unproductive for a bank when the borrower fails to repay it.The proportion of non-performing loans out of the total loans of banks has come down to 1.69 percent. A decline in the proportion of non-performing loans means that banks' loan recovery and credit management are improving. Public sector banks have recorded an improvement in profits for the fifth year in a row. The record profit of Rs 1.09 lakh crore earned by public sector banks in six months, their total business crossing Rs 300 lakh crore and the gross non-performing asset ratio coming down to 1.69% are important milestones that present a positive picture of India's banking sector. Despite all this, if a supreme economic pundit like Rahul Gandhi continues to take potshots at the Modi government over the state of the Indian economy, he certainly deserves nothing less than a Nobel Prize for his intellect.DisclaimerViews expressed above are the author's own.Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

headline: Naveen Patnaik, VK Pandian, and a foreign trips probe that has rocked Odisha politics
content: A probe into the foreign trips undertaken by former Odisha Chief Minister Naveen Patnaik, his close aide and former IAS officer VK Pandian and another IPS officer has triggered a political slugfest between the BJP and the Opposition BJD. In a statement issued on Saturday, the Chief Minister’s Office (CMO) said the inquiry had been ordered following allegations by rights activists that information relating to expenditure on the foreign visits between 2022 and 2024 was “suspicious, non-transparent and incomplete”. The probe will be conducted by S K Vashishth, the Principal Secretary serving in the General Administration Department. The inquiry’s timing too has fuelled political speculation. Coming barely months before the rural and urban local body elections, scheduled for February-March next year, the move is being viewed in the context of the intensifying BJP-BJD contest. The development also comes at a time when the BJD has stepped up its attacks on the BJP government on several fronts. Adding another dimension to the political churn is the increasingly vocal criticism of the government by BJD leader Sujata Karthikeyan, Pandian’s wife, who joined the party in June, months after resigning from the IAS. Patnaik’s foreign visits During his 24-year tenure as Chief Minister, Patnaik undertook three foreign trips. In June 2022, he travelled to Italy and Dubai on an 11-day visit. In Italy, he attended an event organised by the World Food Programme and met Pope Francis at the Vatican City. He also participated in an investors’ meet in Dubai. In April 2023, Patnaik led a business delegation to Japan and Singapore to attract investments to Odisha. Pandian, who was then serving as Patnaik’s private secretary, accompanied him on the visits, as did IPS officer Ravi Kant. Kant, a 1998-batch IPS officer was posted at the Odisha Resident Commissioner’s Office in New Delhi during both trips. He is currently serving as an Inspector-General with the Border Security Force (BSF). Patnaik, who spent much of his early life abroad before entering politics at the age of 51, had made his first foreign visit as Chief Minister to the United Kingdom in 2012, more than 12 years after assuming office. Odisha government sources said information obtained by activists under the Right to Information (RTI) Act about Patnaik’s foreign visits had revealed discrepancies. In response to an RTI application, the Indian Embassy in Rome reportedly said it had made no arrangements for Patnaik’s visit. It also said there had been no correspondence between the Government of India and the embassy in Rome in connection with the trip. “Official records relating to the foreign trips contain incomplete information, while established protocols and procedures appear to have been disregarded during the visits. A detailed inquiry would ascertain whether any illegality was committed during the trips, based on which further legal action can be taken,” an official said requesting anonymity. Political observers, however, remain sceptical about the likely outcome of the inquiry, with some viewing it as a response to the BJP government's difficulties on several fronts. “Had the BJP government been genuinely keen on cornering the BJD leadership and its bureaucrats, it could have pursued several other issues, including the mining and chit fund scams. Instead, it has chosen an issue that is unlikely to yield any significant outcome,” a retired bureaucrat said, requesting anonymity. What prompted the probe? The inquiry is also being seen against the backdrop of growing discontent within sections of the BJP over the government's failure to act on allegations of irregularities during the previous BJD regime. “The BJP leadership had raised several allegations of irregularities during the 2024 elections and promised stringent action against those responsible. Nearly two-and-a-half years later, the government has yet to take decisive action on any of these issues. The BJP cadre, who fought against the BJD on the ground for years, are unhappy with the government,” a BJP leader said. The ruling party has also faced questions over some of its election promises and allegations against the previous government. On the issue of the safety of the Ratna Bhandar, the treasury of the Jagannath Temple in Puri, subsequent findings indicated that the valuables stored inside were safe, weakening some of the claims made by BJP leaders. Despite sweeping the 2024 Lok Sabha elections in the state and securing a majority in the Assembly on its own, the BJP has struggled to make a significant dent in the BJD’s grassroots support base. Patnaik’s vocal criticism Patnaik continues to enjoy considerable public support and has increasingly taken positions that run counter to the BJP’s political interests. These include his support for the Gen Z movement, demand for the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, opposition to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, criticism of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and condemnation of the Delhi Police action against protesters. The BJD has also repeatedly targeted the state government over alleged mismanagement during recent floods, errors in school textbooks, the law and order situation and the pace of development at the grassroots level. BJD spokesperson Lenin Mohanty described the move as “diversionary tactics” intended to deflect attention from the government's failures. “The ruling party is afraid to have a discussion on a host of issues because it has nothing to show. The BJD welcomes the inquiry against the previous government but also demands transparency and accountability in the foreign trips of the incumbent Chief Minister, Deputy Chief Ministers, ministers and senior officials,” he said. Is Karthikeyan in BJP’s crosshairs? The inquiry is also being viewed in the context of Karthikeyan’s growing political profile. Since joining the BJD, she has been vocal in criticising the BJP government on several issues, including the new mining law and its implications for Odisha. She has also described the recent floods as “man-made” and targeted the BJP over the BJD’s performance in campus elections. Her visits to various districts have drawn sizeable crowds, adding to speculation about her emerging role in the Opposition party. Karthikeyan’s entry into the BJD is being viewed by some political observers as part of the party’s longer-term political strategy. Against this backdrop, the inquiry into Pandian’s role in Patnaik’s foreign visits is also being interpreted as an attempt to put pressure on a politically influential figure close to the former Chief Minister. The latest inquiry comes amid earlier allegations relating to Patnaik and Pandian’s helicopter travel. It was alleged that more than Rs 500 crore from the state exchequer had been spent on around 300 helicopter trips by Pandian while he was serving in the CMO. In September, a local court in Khurda dismissed a criminal revision petition filed against Pandian in connection with the allegations, observing that the petitioner had failed to substantiate them. Pandian had also been summoned by the Bhubaneswar Police in connection with an investigation into the alleged disappearance of two inquiry commission reports from the CMO during the previous BJD government's tenure. He responded to the summons through his counsel. The state government subsequently transferred the case to the Crime Branch, but the investigation has made little apparent progress. BJP defends move BJP state president and Rajya Sabha MP Manmohan Samal defended the decision to order the inquiry, saying the government was duty-bound to investigate allegations when they were brought to its notice. “Why is the BJD scared of a probe? If they have done nothing wrong, why are they concerned? Let the inquiry take place. It will bring out the facts,” Samal said. Responding to questions about the timing of the inquiry ahead of the panchayat elections, Samal said the government would initiate a probe only when it found prima facie evidence of wrongdoing.

headline: 4.5K NHM management staff across Odisha demand speedy job regularisation
content: BHUBANESWAR: Uncertainty over the fulfilment of their long-pending demands has triggered widespread discontentment among 4,500 National Health Mission (NHM) management employees across the state.The employees under the Odisha Health Mission Management Employees’ Association alleged that despite repeated assurances from the government, they were still awaiting resolution of their grievances, ranging from regularisation of service and salary disparity to leave provisions and other benefits. They said around 4,500 NHM management employees had been working for over 20 years, handling programme implementation, finance and data management across 8,624 health facilities, ranging from medical colleges to Ayushman Arogya Mandirs. “However, despite our role in strengthening the state’s healthcare delivery system, we continue to remain deprived of many government benefits,” they alleged. The association also raised concern over salary disparity among contractual employees working under the same department. It alleged that management employees were left out while the government increased the salary of others in February. They further pointed out that several states, including Maharashtra, Bihar, Rajasthan, Chhattisgarh and Manipur, have initiated cadre creation and regularisation measures for NHM employees. .“Maharashtra regularised employees who had completed 10 years of service on October 26. However, in Odisha, the first state to regularise around 6,994 contractual employees in 2020, management employees were excluded,” the association alleged.Association president Anirudha Panda said the employees had staged a 25-day agitation at Mahatma Gandhi Marg in March this year, following which assurances were given that their demands would be addressed at the earliest. However, the delay in resolving the issues has left employees increasingly disillusioned, he said.Panda sought creation of public health management cadres and regularisation of the management employees as per the 2017 and 2022 guidelines of the National Health Policy. He also sought the intervention of Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi, saying the process rests with the state government..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

headline: Global Electrical Infrastructure Spending To Reach $32 Trillion Over Next Decade As AI And Power Demand Surge
content: New Delhi: Global spending on electrical infrastructure is projected to reach USD 32 trillion over the next decade, as rising electricity demand from artificial intelligence (AI), electrification and industrial activity drives investment in power generation, grids, storage and critical minerals, according to a UBS report.Also Watch: UBS noted that electricity demand in major developed markets was rising for the first time in decades, even after accounting for efficiency gains. AI infrastructure is adding to demand for power and equipment, while grid modernisation, electric vehicles, industrial automation and the energy transition are also competing for these resources.OpenAI Calls For Common AI Safety Limits, Warns Of Major Breakthroughs By 2027 "We project USD 32tr in global electrical infrastructure spending over the next decade, spanning power generation, grids, storage, and critical minerals," UBS said.The report said the scale of investment could create opportunities for companies operating in areas where supply constraints are most severe.Businesses with limited production capacity, established order books, strong customer relationships and a track record of executing complex projects are likely to be better positioned to benefit.Vaishali Verma Steps Down As Initiative India CEO, Ends Leadership Stint To Explore New Opportunities "We think the most profitable potential opportunities from this trend exist where supply-side constraints are tightest, providing strong pricing power and unprecedented visibility to future revenues," the report said.UBS also projected global grid investment at USD 500 billion in 2026, with annual investment across the sector potentially approaching USD 3 trillion by 2030.However, the report cautioned that companies in the sector could face risks from rising financing costs, higher input prices, delays in obtaining permits and the pace of data centre construction.Gold Prices Fall ₹65 Lakh Per Kg, Delhi Traders' Body CTI Thanks PM Modi For Warning Against Buying At High Rates The report also highlighted copper as a key beneficiary of rising infrastructure demand. Power networks, electrification, data centres and AI infrastructure are expected to require substantial quantities of the metal.UBS said supply was responding slowly to rising demand, as new mines take a long time to develop, ore grades are declining in several established mining regions and large projects face political, environmental and execution-related challenges. It expects copper prices to reach USD 15,500 per tonne by the end of 2027.The report said the scale and duration of the electrical infrastructure investment cycle could be greater than markets currently anticipate, although financing and supply-side constraints remain important risks.
