headline: Manipur CM assures assistance to victims of spurious liquor tragedy
content: Manipur Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh on Monday assured tribal civil society organisations (CSOs) that the state government would extend all possible assistance to the families of the victims of the spurious liquor tragedy and their affected families. At least 17 persons have died so far, while around 230 others are undergoing treatment at various hospitals in Manipur since November 18 after consuming suspected spurious liquor in Manipur's two districts. The incident has claimed 17 lives -- 16 in Chandel District and one in Kakching District. A senior official of the Chief Minister’s Office (CMO) said that the Chief Minister on Monday met representatives of various Anal Tribes’ CSOs to discuss the recent suspected spurious liquor tragedy in Chandel District and Kakching District. The representatives apprised the Chief Minister of the situation arising out of the tragic incident and submitted a memorandum seeking immediate intervention of the state government. The memorandum highlighted the need for compensation to the bereaved families, full medical assistance to all affected persons, strengthening of healthcare infrastructure in Chandel district and rehabilitation support for the affected families. It also sought the constitution of a Special Investigation Team (SIT) headed by an officer of Inspector General of Police (IGP) Manipur rank to ensure a thorough investigation into the incident and bring those responsible to justice. Responding to the demands raised by the representatives, Khemchand Singh informed them that a High-Level Enquiry Committee has been constituted, headed by Principal Secretary, R.K. Dinesh Singh, to conduct an enquiry into the tragedy. The Chief Minister expressed concern over the tragic loss of lives and assured the representatives that the government would look into the issues raised in the memorandum.

headline: What stands atop Thirupparankundram hill is a survey pillar, ascertains Tamil Nadu government report
content: CHENNAI A 2026 report compiled by the Departments of Survey and Settlement and Archaeology of the Tamil Nadu government ascertains that the pillar near the Sikandar Badusha Dargah in Thirupparankundram hill is a Great Trigonometrical Survey (GTS) pillar erected by the British. The map prepared by the Departments identifies the original Deepathoon (lamp pillar) to be below the dargah. Click here to read the full report by Tamil Nadu government on the Thiruppankundram pillar https://www.thehindu.com/news/resources/71739213-thirupparankundram-deepathohttps:/www.thehindu.com/news/resources/71739213-thirupparankundram-deepathoon-a-survey-pillar-says-tn-govt-report-pdfon-a-survey-pillar-says-tn-govt-report-pdf This report has evoked interest against the backdrop of the latest dispute over the lighting of the Karthigai Deepam atop Thirupparankundram hill has taken centre stage, following the Supreme Court’s decision to permit the lighting of the lamp at the newly identified deepathoon as a limited, one-time arrangement. Supreme Court allows lighting of lamp on deepathoon at Thirupparankundram as limited one-time arrangement storyline 1 Thirupparankundram row: when politics invades a syncretic hill town Thirupparankundram row: when politics invades a syncretic hill town In Thirupparankundram in Madurai, Hindus and Muslims live in camaraderie, but that has not kept the hill, which holds a couple of temples, a dargah, and some Jain beds, out of dispute. Here, we outline the history of judgments involving different petitioners through the years, in an attempt to understand the current crisis. THE SUNDAY STORY Thirupparankundram row: when politics invades a syncretic hill town storyline 1 The report says the triangulation bearings from Sikandarmalai hill station (Tiruparankundrum) to other stations such as Nagamalai, Sadragiri, Gopalswami, Kutiparai, Madurai temple (Meenakshi Amman temple), Ponurikimalai and Perumalmalai, taken in the present survey, are consistent with values given in the GTS report of the colonial period. “These values suggest that the pillar installed at Sikandarmalai and the associated station marks engraved in situ on the rocky surface having circle with a dot is a survey pillar,” says the report prepared by officials from the Survey and Settlement and Archaeology Departments. Also read: Thirupparankundram row LIVE updates https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/tamil-nadu/karthigai-deepam-deepathoon-lighting-2026-live-updates-november-24-tamil-nadu/article71737406.ece In the five-volume report, running over 1,800 pages, more than 800 stations were identified in the survey’s first phase. Of these, 484 stations, comprising 210 primary and 274 secondary stations, were physically documented. Thirupparankundram was a secondary station with stone pillar and stone mark. The report was based on the order issued by the Revenue and Disaster Management Department of Tamil Nadu in December 2025, to systematically identify and document all GTS stations. In August, 2026, the Revenue Department granted permission to publish the report. The Department of Survey and Settlement comes under the administrative control of the Revenue and Disaster Management Department. In the Survey, stations were established through triangulation, which involves measuring angles between contiguous points relative to a baseline. Landscapes with hills provided clear lines of sight, making it easier to fix triangulation points, whereas flat areas required more stations due to limited visibility. Karthigai Deepam lit only at deepa mandapam for over 150 years: Tamil Nadu government tells Supreme Court Karthigai Deepam lit only at deepa mandapam for over 150 years: Tamil Nadu government tells Supreme Court There has never existed any established practice, custom, or even a prior claim of lighting the Karthigai Deepam on the summit of the Thirupparankundram Hill or at the stone pillar “now described as the deepathoon”, says govt. Karthigai Deepam lit only at deepa mandapam for over 150 years: Tamil Nadu government tells Supreme Court storyline 1 The order says that historically, survey stations and control points were meticulously marked on GTS maps, topo sheets, and village maps, and served as anchors for cartography and land management. However, the passage of time, coupled with rapid and often unplanned urbanisation, terrain change due to natural calamities, extensive industrialisation, and unfortunately, instances of human vandalism, rendered many of these original physical station points untraceable. According to the order, the Director of Survey and Settlement proposed to undertake a comprehensive field exercise to systematically identify, map, document, and preserve all GTS stations in Tamil Nadu, and to use their coordinates to conduct subsequent surveys in the State.

headline: Commerce dept urges DRI to release confiscated bulk Scotch from UK
content: The commerce and industry ministry has requested the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) to release shipments of bulk Scotch imports from the United Kingdom (UK) confiscated by Indian Customs following a tariff classification dispute. The ministry is engaged with the revenue department to find a ‘technical solution’ to the Customs tariff classification issue under the India-UK trade deal that came into effect from July 15. “In our conversation with the UK authorities, we have indicated very clearly that the commitment is as given under the CETA (Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement). This is something we have also engaged with the UK companies or local importers,” Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal told reporters on Monday. Explaining the issue, Agrawal said that while concessions on bulk Scotch were given under the tariff code — 220830 — under the trade deal, some imports have been happening under a different code of 220890 — which is not entitled to lower preferential tariffs under the trade deal. The imports were happening under the 220890 code following court orders dating back to 1991. The commerce department is actively seeking a view to resolve the matter in the next few days. Indian Customs have seized stocks from major liquor companies from the UK, claiming buyers are trying to avail the 75 per cent lower import duty offered under the trade deal by using the wrong tariff line. Bulk Scotch whiskey is typically imported into India from the UK for local blending and bottling. According to the India-UK trade deal, the preferential import duty for bulk Scotch whiskey was cut from 150 per cent to 75 per cent on the first day of the FTA and will gradually reduce to 40 per cent over 10 years. “Our understanding (during the negotiations) was that bulk scotch was imported under the HSN code 220830. We have been pointed out that bulk Scotch also used to come under the 220890 code and the genesis of this has to do with certain legal judgement in the past, wherein the importing industry has gone into the court stating that they want to import under the code 220890 and not under 220830,” said Agrawal, adding that these cases went up to the Supreme Court and it was confirmed. “Finding a technical solution also required that we won’t go against the court’s order, while making sure that the concessions given under the deal is also respected,” he added.

headline: India's informal sector rebounds in Q2FY27 led by rural recovery: NSO
content: The unincorporated non-farm sector rebounded in July-September, with the number of enterprises as well as the workforce strength expanding sequentially by 9.2 per cent and 9.7 per cent, respectively, according to the “Quarterly Bulletin of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises”, released by the National Statistics Office (NSO) on Monday. This marks a turnaround from April-June, when establishments contracted by 5.4 per cent and the workforce by 9.7 per cent quarter-on-quarter (Q-o-Q), the steepest decline since the NSO began releasing quarterly unincorporated enterprise data in January-March 2025. With the rebound, the establishment count climbed to 94.7 million, the highest in the series. The number of workers reached its second-highest level at 150.2 million during the same period. The recovery was led by rural India, which had accounted for much of the decline in the previous quarter. Between the first and second quarters this financial year, rural establishments rose 12.3 per cent and the rural workforce 11.2 per cent. Urban areas’ gains were comparatively modest, with the establishment base rising 6 per cent and workers 8.4 per cent. Trade saw the sharpest sequential rebound, with establishments rising 14.9 per cent and workers 14.7 per cent quarter-on-quarter (Q-o-Q), after falling 11.2 per cent and 12 per cent, respectively, in April-June. Establishments coming under “Other Services” grew 7.9 per cent, while their workforce rose 9.7 per cent, reversing the 6.7 per cent decline of the previous quarter. Establishments in manufacturing increased 5.8 per cent and their workforce 4.1 per cent, partly reversing the declines of 8.6 per cent and 12.1 per cent seen in the first quarter. The composition of employment, meanwhile, continued to tilt towards self-employment on a yearly basis. Working owners rose to 62 per cent of all workers in July-September, up from 60 per cent a year earlier, while hired workers slipped to 23.2 per cent from 25.9 per cent. Sequentially, however, the trend reversed. Between the first and second quarters, the working-owner share fell 0.4 percentage points, while the hired-worker share rose 0.45 percentage points. The number of hired workers rose to an estimated 34.9 million from 31.2 million in the previous quarter, an increase of nearly 12 per cent. Further, digitisation continued to deepen during the quarter. About 83.7 per cent of the establishments reported using the internet, compared to 82.2 per cent in the previous quarter. The share of establishments using online financial services, including Unified Payments Interface (UPI), remained broadly unchanged at 79.8 per cent as against 79.9 per cent in the first. Additionally, female workers accounted for 31.22 per cent of employment in the second quarter, compared to 30.56 per cent in the first.

headline: Delhi man called to police station for counselling goes on stabbing spree, injures 9 cops
content: “Who filed a complaint against me?” Around 2:30 pm on Monday, Nabeel, 30, entered the Jama Masjid police station, allegedly bitter and enraged. He had been summoned for a counselling session to resolve a family dispute. As he directed his anger towards the police officers, allegedly using a slew of expletives, Sub-Inspector Ajay walked up to pacify him. Suddenly, Nabeel took out a knife and stabbed him, taking him by surprise, according to police. He then went on a stabbing spree and five policemen were attacked with that knife. He then made an escape bid and a police chase followed. He then allegedly stabbed four more personnel before the team was able to tackle him. With an encounter ending the chase, he was injured in the leg as shots were fired and six bullets hit his legs. How the attack unfolded A police officer who was present at the police station said that Nabeel had been unemployed for a long time, and was taking money from his sister and mother. The duo claimed that Nabeel used to beat them, which is why they were there to file a complaint. They were at the police station when Nabeel arrived on Monday afternoon. DCP Rohit Rajbir Singh said. “Nabeel had been called to the police station for counselling after a complaint was filed by his mother and sister, alleging that he was troubling them." After Nabeel allegedly started abusing police officers, SI Ajay snapped back at him. An officer said that when Nabeel proceeded towards him, SI Ajay assumed that he would just push him. Another senior police officer added, “During an interaction with the police personnel, the accused suddenly pulled out a knife and attacked him. Other staff present inside the police station came to the officer’s rescue, but Nabeel stabbed four others one after another causing injuries to their faces and necks.” Sub-Inspector Ajay, Sub-Inspector Arvind and Head Constable Harender sustained serious injuries. Assistant Sub-Inspector Shri Krishna and Head Constable Baljeet were also injured. All five injured personnel were shifted to Sir Ganga Ram Hospital for treatment. The rampage made the other officers alert, who then tried to pacify him from a distance. Taking advantage of the situation, Nabeel allegedly dashed out of the police station. Outside the police station, the 30-year-old allegedly stopped a scooter rider, forced him off the vehicle, and drove at least a kilometre away towards Chitli Qabar area. Officers said that police personnel from the Anti-Auto Theft Squad (AATS) called him and started chasing Nabeel. He was finally intercepted near Chitli Qabar near the Chandni Mahal area of Old Delhi. Nabeel then took out his knife, again, they added. “Around 4:30 pm, when the police team attempted to apprehend him, the accused again went on stabbing spree, injuring four members of the Special Staff, namely Constable Ankit, Constable Jayant, Constable Lokesh and Constable Parminder. The injured personnel were shifted to LNJP Hospital for treatment,” said DCP Singh. The Special Staff in Delhi Police consists of district-level investigative and operational units that track fugitives, bust organised gangs, and solve serious or complex crimes within their respective police districtsThe team of policemen then took out their guns and started firing. Eight rounds were fired towards Nabeel and six bullets hit his legs. Nabeel was finally nabbed and taken to a hospital. Investigation revealed that Nabeel has a history of violent bursts of attacks. “Nabeel has a previous case of causing hurt registered at the Daryaganj police station,” said another officer.

headline: Amritpal Singh’s grandmother’s bhog held in Jalupur Khera; uncle attends ceremony on parole
content: The bhog ceremony of the Sehaj Path held in memory of Charan Kaur, grandmother of Khadoor Sahib MP Amritpal Singh, was held at a gurdwara in Jalupur Khera village on Monday.It was attended by a large number of prominent religious, political and social figures. Amritpal Singh’s uncle, Harjit Singh, who is lodged in Bathinda jail, also attended the ceremony on parole.Punjab Congress president and MP Amarinder Singh Raja Warring visited the village to offer condolences to the family. Parminder Singh Dhindsa of the SAD (Punar Surjit) faction also attended the bhog ceremony.Representatives of religious organisations, Sikh sects, farmer groups, Panthic organisations and political parties joined the prayers and expressed condolences to the family. A written condolence message from Jagtar Singh Hawara, who is lodged in jail in connection with the Beant Singh assassination case, was also brought to the ceremony.In his message, Hawara expressed grief over Charan Kaur’s demise and extended his condolences to the family, praying for strength for them to bear the loss.Condolence messages were also sent by Delhi Sikh Gurdwara Management Committee president Harmeet Singh Kalka and Jathedar Balbir Singh of Kar Sewa.Among those who attended the ceremony were MP Sarabjit Singh Khalsa, MLA Manpreet Singh Ayali, former MLA Iqbal Singh Jhunda, Ajmer Singh, Amarjit Singh Vanchiri and Baljit Singh Khalsa.Amritpal Singh’s father, Tarsem Singh, thanked the congregation and all those who attended the ceremony and stood by the family during their hour of grief.

headline: Warring’s visit to Amritpal’s grandmother’s bhog sparks buzz in Punjab Congress
content: Former Punjab Congress chief Amrinder Singh Raja Warring’s presence at the bhog ceremony of Khadoor Sahib MP Amritpal Singh’s grandmother, Charan Kaur, has triggered political curiosity, particularly in view of his earlier public criticism of the jailed MP.Warring, along with former Zira MLA Kulbir Zira, former PPCC general secretary (organisation) Capt Sandeep Sandhu, and Rajbir Bhullar, Taran Taran district president, attended the bhog ceremony and interacted with Tarsem Singh, father of Amritpal, at Jallupur Khera village in Amritsar.The Ludhiana MP said there was nothing political to read into the visit. “I had gone to pay respects to the departed soul. I have spoken on the issue of Bandi Singhs in Parliament.”PPCC chief Pargat Singh said there was nothing wrong with Warring attending the bhog ceremony. “I have always said the sentencing of Amritpal should be according to the law. The law should be the same for all.”In party circles, Warring’s visit has raised many eyebrows. The Congress, as a party, had in February 2023 condemned Amritpal Singh’s pro-Khalistan stand and the storming of the Ajnala police station. But over the past year, former CM Charanjit Singh Channi has been quite vocal about the release of Amritpal. Channi had also been praised by Amritpal’s father for standing up for his son.A section of party leaders believe Warring’s move was aimed at Channi, as he seeks to exert his influence in Punjab’s changing political spectrum, where Amritpal’s party, Akali Dal Waris Punjab De, could play a crucial role.

headline: HC frames time-bound guidelines for upgrading infrastructure at AIIMS Deoghar
content: Ranchi, Nov 23 (PTI) The Jharkhand High Court on Monday framed guidelines for the government in order to develop better infrastructure in the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) in Deoghar. The court also set a six-month deadline for the government to execute the directions of the bench. A division bench comprising Chief Justice MS Sonak and Justice Manoj Prasad was hearing a public interest litigation filed by Godda MP Nishikant Dubey for providing better facilities in the hospital. The court asked the government to ensure commissioning of an electricity grid sub-station for supply of power to the hospital. Besides, a high-speed diesel storage tank will also be constructed on the campus within three months for providing fuel to the generators so that the hospital can get uninterrupted power supply. The bench also directed the government to conduct a fire audit of the hospital to check on fire safety in the hospital. The court also ordered the district administration and the government to clear encroachment in and around the hospital premises. The court cautioned the government that mere correspondence and letters will not be accepted as compliance with the orders of the bench, the judges said. The matter will be heard again on May 13, 2027, by which time the government will have to finish construction of the infrastructure required for running the Hospital. headline: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO after U.S. government input
content: New York Nvidia on Monday (November 23, 2026) reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive after input from senior U.S. government officials left its board confident he posed no national security risk, less than two weeks after the co-founder resigned due to an alleged spy scandal. Jensen Huang | AI rainmaker meets his Waterloo storyline 1 U.S. President Donald Trump welcomed the move as a “correct and proper decision.” Wall Street roars back as Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO Wall Street roars back as Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO Nvidia shares surged 32.2%, on track for their biggest one-day jump in more than two decades after an extraordinary reversal, which followed President Donald Trump’s call for Jensen Huang’s return Wall Street roars back as Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO storyline 1 The board voted unanimously to bring Mr. Huang back as president, chief executive and board member, effective immediately, after a series of meetings left directors satisfied with his “candor and ability to lead”, the company said in a statement. Nvidia did not name the government officials it consulted or say what they told the board. Jensen Huang returns as Nvidia CEO: 6 other CEOs who reclaimed their top positions https://www.thehindu.com/sci-tech/technology/jensen-huang-reinstated-in-nvidia-other-ceos-who-reclaimed-positions/article71737407.ece The decision came three days after Mr. Trump publicly urged Nvidia to take Mr. Huang back, calling him “one of the truly most brilliant minds in the world” and saying he would “love to see Jensen be given a second chance.” Was Jensen Huang given the Jack Ma treatment? | The View from India podcast Was Jensen Huang given the Jack Ma treatment? | The View from India podcast In this episode, Ananth Krishnan examines the controversy surrounding Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, the U.S.-China battle over AI and semiconductors, and the parallels with Jack Ma’s experience. Was Jensen Huang given the Jack Ma treatment? | The View from India podcast audio 1 Mr. Trump described Mr. Huang as “a good man” who “made some bad decisions" and said the company should rehire him “if they were smart". Mr. Huang had offered to return, but the board initially refused. Board chair Harvey Jones had said on an earnings call last week that directors had unanimously accepted his resignation and did “not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO". “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment,” Mr. Huang said, thanking the board, staff, shareholders and his family. “I can’t wait to get back to work.” Mr. Huang, 63, stepped down on November 12 following reports that he had a relationship with Alice Huang — no relation — a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a company that bought billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips. U.S. intelligence services reportedly concluded she passed information to Beijing, which has denied the allegations. Board chair Harvey Jones said on Monday (November 23, 2026) that directors now believe Mr. Huang “is the right person to lead Nvidia” and that his return serves the interests of shareholders, employees, partners and customers. Jones, a former Synopsys chief executive who was named Nvidia’s first-ever board chair during the crisis, will stay in the role. Chief financial officer Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO, will continue as CFO. Nvidia said a committee of independent directors set up earlier this month to investigate whether Mr. Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort will see its probe through to the end. Huang supports the investigation and has committed to cooperating, the company said.

headline: 8-year-old mauled to death by stray dogs on way to school in Amritsar’s Jandiala Guru
content: An eight-year-old boy was mauled to death by a pack of stray dogs in Jalal village in the Jandiala Guru constituency on Monday.The victim, Ranjit Singh, was on his way to school when the dogs chased him into a vacant plot and attacked him. He was the only son of his parents and the youngest of four siblings.According to family members, Ranjit ran into the vacant plot in an attempt to escape, but the pack cornered him and mauled him.His body was found by children who had come to the plot to play. They informed the villagers and the family, who rushed to the spot. The dogs had inflicted severe injuries on his head and legs and had bitten off his right ear.ASI Jaspal Singh said the police reached the spot and took possession of the body.The incident has left the village in mourning, with residents demanding adequate compensation for the bereaved family and urgent steps by the government and district administration to tackle the stray dog menace.The incident has once again highlighted the issue of stray dog attacks, particularly in rural areas, where residents allege a lack of effective measures to control the stray dog population.Earlier this year, the Supreme Court directed high courts to initiate suo motu proceedings to monitor compliance with its directions on stray dogs, including setting up shelters and dog pounds, establishing Animal Birth Control centres in every district, and providing vaccination and medical facilities. The court had also directed authorities to take legally permissible measures in cases involving rabid, incurably ill, or demonstrably dangerous and aggressive dogs. It warned that officials failing to comply with its directions could face contempt proceedings and other appropriate action.The court had observed that citizens, particularly children and the elderly, could not be left exposed to the threat of dog attacks.

headline: BJP government decides to rename West Bengal – ‘Paschim Banga’ – after failed bids by Left, TMC
content: After the failed attempts by the previous Left Front and Trinamool Congress governments to change the name of West Bengal, the BJP government has decided to rename the state ‘Paschim Banga’. A resolution to this effect will be tabled in the Winter Session of the Assembly, which will begin on December 4. The decision was taken at a Cabinet meeting, chaired by Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari at Nabanna, the state secretariat. “In English, we will write our state's name exactly the way we say it in Bengali, that is, Paschim Banga. We will introduce a resolution in the Assembly on December 9. After that, we will send the passed resolution to the Central government,” the chief minister told mediapersons after the Cabinet meeting. Once approved by the Union Home Ministry, the state's name will be written as ‘Paschim Banga’ in English as well, instead of ‘West Bengal’, across official documents and administrative records. With the BJP in power in both West Bengal and at the Centre, experts believe the latest renaming effort is unlikely to face major hurdles. From W to P – the burden of alphabetical order The state has long faced administrative inconvenience because the initial letter 'W' in 'West Bengal' places it towards the end of the alphabetical order in English. At meetings of chief ministers in Delhi and other all-India administrative gatherings, West Bengal's representatives often get the opportunity to speak towards the end of proceedings because of the alphabetical listing of states. The latest effort to change the name is partly aimed at addressing this issue, officials said. The failed bids of Buddhadeb, Mamata The issue was first raised during the chief ministership of Siddhartha Shankar Ray in 1974 when the Congress was in power. Several names came up in the past — Bangla, Bango, Bangodesh, Bangopradesh, Bangobhumi to name a few. But the first concrete attempt was made in 1999 when Buddhadeb Bhattacharjee was chief minister. The Left Front government then came up with the name ‘Bangla”. A proposal to rename the state was discussed in the Assembly on July 20, 1999, but the debate did not make much headway. After coming to power in 2011, the Trinamool Congress government of Mamata Banerjee got a resolution passed unanimously in the Assembly on September 2 that year, recommending that the state's name be changed to 'Paschim Banga' in English as well, and sent the proposal to the Centre. Initially, the Congress-led UPA government at the Centre had informed the state government that a Bill — West Bengal (Alteration of Name) Act, 2014 —would be tabled in Parliament. However, the Bill was never tabled in the House. Five years later, on August 29, 2016, the state Assembly passed a second resolution proposing three names in three languages – 'Bangla' in Bengali, 'Bengal' in English and 'Bangal' in Hindi. However, the BJP government at the Centre, led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, rejected the state government’s proposal, stating that it was not constitutionally permissible for a state to have different names in three languages. Accepting the Centre's objection, the TMC government passed a third resolution in the Assembly on July 26, 2018. This time, it proposed that the state be called 'Bangla' in Bengali, English and Hindi, and sent the proposal to Delhi. But the Centre did not approve the proposal, saying the name resembled Bangladesh. The Centre, reportedly, argued that the name 'Bangla' bore a strong resemblance to that of the neighbouring country, which could confuse the international diplomatic level and in various global forums. A section of the Bengal BJP also strongly opposed the name 'Bangla', citing the historical context of Bengal's partition and the painful memories associated with it. The BJP had then argued that the name 'West Bengal' was linked to the history of Partition and should not be erased. With the BJP government at the Centre withholding its approval, the initiative was eventually put on the back burner by the TMC government. With PTI Inputs

headline: No government support for running open-weight AI models, says Sarvams co-founder amid Chinese models row
content: New Delhi [India], November 23 (ANI): Amid growing controversy over the use of Chinese-developed artificial intelligence (AI) models by Indian startup Sarvam, its co-founder Pratyush Kumar has clarified that the company's Token Factory platform operates on privately procured computing infrastructure without government support, while subsidies received under the IndiaAI Mission were utilised to develop its indigenous AI model.The clarification comes amid questions over Sarvam's decision to offer Chinese-developed AI models through its commercial platform, despite being among the startups supported under the government's Rs 10,370-crore IndiaAI Mission, aimed at strengthening India's domestic artificial intelligence capabilities and reducing dependence on foreign technology.In a post on social media platform X, Kumar explained that the government's support was provided in the form of subsidised access to graphics processing units (GPUs) for developing indigenous foundation models and was not used to finance Sarvam's commercial inference operations."The government did not pay Sarvam directly, instead like with every supported startup, the subsidy went to GPU cloud providers, helping seed AI infra in the country," Kumar said.According to Kumar, around 20 startups received subsidised access to computing infrastructure under the IndiaAI Mission, with the government providing a 40 per cent discount on GPU computing costs.He said Sarvam utilised this support to train its proprietary Sarvam 105B model from scratch, which was subsequently made available as an open-weight model.Addressing concerns over the company's commercial operations, Kumar said, "Sarvam Token Factory is one of the first large inference offerings in India. We serve multiple open-weight models on GPUs we have privately procured, without any government support."He further highlighted that the company had optimised its infrastructure to offer AI inference services at costs comparable to, or lower than, established international providers.The controversy has brought renewed attention to India's AI sovereignty ambitions, particularly the question of whether domestic AI self-reliance should focus exclusively on developing indigenous foundation models or also include operating foreign-developed models on computing infrastructure located within the country.Sarvam's Token Factory, launched earlier this month, offers access to several open-weight AI models through infrastructure based in India, including models developed by Chinese companies such as DeepSeek, Alibaba, Moonshot AI and Z.ai.The presence of Chinese-developed models on the platform has raised questions about the use of government-supported computing resources and the broader objectives of India's sovereign AI programme.However, Kumar maintained that the government-backed computing resources were used for developing Sarvam's indigenous model, while Token Factory's commercial inference infrastructure was funded privately.In its official announcement on November 16, Sarvam said Token Factory was designed to provide competitive AI inference services while addressing requirements for domestic computing infrastructure, lower latency and cost efficiency.The company claimed that the platform was already processing more than 450 billion tokens daily through DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, with 95.7 per cent of prompt tokens served from cache.According to Sarvam, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash was offered at Rs 14 per million input tokens and Rs 55 per million output tokens on its standard offering.The company also announced an improved version of its proprietary model, Sarvam 105B-1711, with enhanced reasoning, tool-calling and Indian-language capabilities, and output pricing of Rs 25 per million tokens.Kumar maintained that developing indigenous AI models and building commercially viable inference infrastructure were complementary objectives rather than competing priorities."Building inference capability does not conflict with our core mission: training our own models," he said.Highlighting India's dependence on overseas AI services, Kumar said, "Today, India consumes a few trillion tokens a day and imports the majority of them."Sarvam also plans to introduce additional models for vision, speech and edge AI while expanding its domestic computing capabilities.Kumar acknowledged that developing globally competitive AI models would require investments running into hundreds of millions, and eventually billions, of dollars."We firmly believe that India can and must win across the full-stack of AI," he said. (ANI)(This content is sourced from a syndicated feed and is published as received. The Tribune assumes no responsibility or liability for its accuracy, completeness, or content.)

headline: How just one ingredient can make ‘fairness’ creams dangerous for health
content: A 17-year-old girl from Keralam developed a kidney disease called membranous nephropathy and was hospitalised after she used a so-called fairness cream with alarmingly high levels of mercury. Keralam Health Minister K Muraleedharan on Sunday (November 22) ordered stringent action against the sale of illegal cosmetic products and protein powders, as well as those who promote them through social media. He also said that some of these creams were coming from Pakistan. Earlier this month, Madhya Pradesh also cracked down on unauthorised Pakistan-made ‘whitening’ creams. What happened in this case, what makes such creams potentially harmful, and how does the government regulate them? The Keralam case The girl purchased a fairness cream from an e-commerce platform after a vlogger recommended it. After she complained of swelling on the body (edema), bubbly urine and other symptoms, she was taken to the Aster MIMS Hospital at Areekode in Malappuram. She was then diagnosed with membranous nephropathy, a medical condition in which the immune system damages the glomeruli, or the tiny filtering units of the kidneys. The resulting injury allows proteins, particularly albumin, to escape into urine. The patient’s history showed that she has been using a fairness cream, whose samples were tested outside the state and found to have high mercury levels. Several people have since shared similar experiences on social media. Prevalence in Keralam According to Dr S Gouri, a nephrologist who diagnosed the girl’s case, the Aster MIMS hospital at Kottakkal (in Malappuram district) alone reported 13 similar cases between 2021 and 2023. The patients had purchased creams over the counter or via online platforms. She said nephrologists in the state have been made aware of the issue for the last five years, due to kidney-related ailments caused by high-mercury cosmetics. The issue has also been debated at a state-level conference of nephrologists. In such cases, recovery may take three months to a year. Dr Gouri said that most patients were young and middle-aged, and none reportedly underwent dialysis. The disease does not turn fatal mainly because of early diagnosis, as the intense symptoms force patients to consult nephrologists. Why is mercury added to fairness products? The permitted level of mercury in such cosmetics is 1 ppm, but the mercury content found in this cream’s sample was around 12,500 ppm. Skin care products sometimes contain mercury, which functions as a lightening agent due to its ability to inhibit melanin production. Melanin is a pigment produced naturally by the body to protect the skin against the sun’s ultraviolet rays, and it results in darker skin and hair colour. Once applied to the skin, mercury inactivates tyrosinase, an enzyme that supports melanin production. Higher tyrosinase activity produces more melanin, resulting in darker skin, while low activity does the reverse. When incorporated in a cream, mercury is easily absorbed into the skin and spreads throughout the body. According to the US FDA, mercury absorption can cause kidney damage, potentially leading to rapid kidney failure, as well as neurological damage such as tremors, tingling or numbness, headaches, fatigue, and mood or cognitive disturbances. What rules govern cosmetics in India? The Union Health Ministry implemented the Cosmetic Rules of 2020 for a separate legal framework for the industry and to protect consumer interests. Cosmetics were earlier under the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945. Section 39 (5) of the Cosmetic Rules fixes the “level of unintentional mercury” in cosmetic products at 1 ppm. For products meant for around the eye, the level should not exceed seventy parts per million (0.007%). The rules also state that product labels should disclose any hazardous or poisonous ingredients, while the inner label must have a statement indicating the exact names and quantities of those ingredients. Creams purchased online often lack ingredient labels. Both the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation under the Union Government and state drug control departments have different roles in governing the cosmetics industry. The central body monitors imports, approves new products with novel ingredients, and sets national safety standards, while the state body issues licenses to domestic manufacturers, inspects factories, and monitors retail markets against spurious or unsafe products. According to Kerala’s drugs control department, a special drive held in July this year against the illegal sale of cosmetic products (mainly fairness creams and lipstick) led to 15 cases being registered and cosmetics worth Rs 4 lakhs being seized. These cases were registered after a raid in the domestic market and most were against traders who sold products without a manufacturing license. High levels of mercury were detected in two fairness creams, with a content of up to 15,000 ppm. Lab reports are awaited for further action. Since 2025, the department has also conducted awareness drives among higher secondary school students. Across over 334 sessions, with each camp having at least 50 students, students have been made aware of harmful fairness creams and lipsticks containing toxins. Globally, the Minamata Convention was adopted in 2013 under the United Nations Environmental Programme to protect human life from the health hazards of mercury. Named after the Japanese city of Minamata, where mercury poisoning had been a major issue, the treaty is envisaged to phase out/control the use of mercury in consumer/skin care products, among other objectives. Article 4 of the convention requires all parties not to allow the manufacture, import or export of cosmetics (with mercury content above 1ppm), including skin lightening soaps and creams. India ratified the convention in 2018.

headline: 'Why wait till 2030': AAP questions Delhi government's '60 per cent Yamuna clean' claim
content: New Delhi: AAP Delhi unit president Saurabh Bharadwaj on Monday questioned Environment Minister Manjinder Singh Sirsa's claim that 60 per cent of the Yamuna had been cleaned, alleging the 2030 deadline for cleaning the river was aimed at avoiding accountability before the next Delhi Assembly elections. ."60 per cent of Yamuna ji is totally clean… Clean means so clean that even you can drink that water," Sirsa had said, urging people to visit the river and see the improvement themselves. He also said the entire river would be cleaned by 2029 or 2030. .Responding to the minister's remarks, Bharadwaj said if 60 per cent of the river could be cleaned in 18 months, the remaining 40 per cent should be cleaned in the next 12 months. .Speaking at the launch of Uber's "One Less Car" report in Delhi earlier in the day, Sirsa credited Chief Minister Rekha Gupta and the Centre's support over the last two years for the progress in cleaning the river. .He said the cleaning work had started from one end of the river and would gradually move towards the other, explaining why the entire stretch had not yet been covered. .Bharadwaj questioned the government's timeline of 2030, alleging it would allow the BJP government to avoid questions over the river's condition before the next Assembly elections. .Sirsa also noted that sewage flowing through drains into the Yamuna remained a major challenge and stressed that the river could not be cleaned without treating the city's sewage. .He said the government was using sewage treatment plants (STPs) to address the issue.

headline: Can Congress Turn Anti-AAP Sentiment Into A Comeback in Punjab?
content: ASSEMBLY ELECTION 2027 On November 4, Rahul Gandhi returned to Punjab, a State where the Congress party has historically known how to sway voters and win elections. Launching the campaign for the Punjab Assembly elections in Sangrur, an Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) stronghold, Rahul attacked the AAP’s record in government and argued that Punjab needed a government that worked for the State rather than being “run from Delhi”. The rally came at a time when the Congress, the ruling party in only one northern State, Himachal Pradesh, is trying to add momentum to its national-level recovery with a win in a State that had once been its stronghold. Also, after improving its Lok Sabha tally from 44 seats in 2014 to 99 in 2024, the party has increasingly sought to project Rahul as a more assertive opposition leader, taking on the Modi government. But in Punjab, Rahul’s pitch was not simply an extension of that national campaign. His appeal to sentiments around Punjab’s distinct political identity builds on an older Congress-Punjab relationship. For much of its post-Independence history, the Congress remained one of the principal political forces in Punjab as its journey intertwined with some of the many consequential changes in the border State. The party’s fortunes declined elsewhere following the BJP’s Modi wave, which swept away many of the Congress’ traditional strongholds after 2014. Yet Punjab, which brought the Congress back to power as recently as 2017, managed to buck the trend. But voters in this outlier State have always shown little preference for continuity, which often results in the incumbent ruling party’s ouster. This happened in 2022 when the AAP mopped up 92 of Punjab’s 117 Assembly seats. The Congress, with just 18 seats, was roundly defeated. The State’s voters had built a new consensus that created a third political front. https://frontline.thehindu.com/cover-story/punjab-assembly-election-results-aap-expansion/article38454244.ece “In 2022, the AAP was the only party that came into the fray without any baggage from the past,” said Sikander Singh, head of Misal Baba Sawan Singh Attari Dharna Dal, a Nihang Sikh group. “The driving force, which persuaded us to vote for it, was the AAP’s Delhi governance model, which had seemingly brought some relief to people there.” However, with the passage of time, the ground beneath the AAP’s feet shifted. In the 2024 Lok Sabha election, it won only 3 seats while the Congress bagged 7 of the State’s 13 parliamentary constituencies. Growing popular disenchantment with the AAP government, which started drawing criticism well before the general election, was perceived to be the cause of this reversal. From governance issues to religious matters, Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann’s government has repeatedly found itself cornered. https://frontline.thehindu.com/politics/aap-akal-takht-punjab-politics-bhagwant-mann/article71196874.ece Two years after the 2024 election, the AAP is out of power in Delhi and faces strong anti-incumbency in Punjab. Many observers believe that the situation creates a window for the AAP’s political opponents. With the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) struggling to recover its lost credibility and the BJP yet to establish a strong political base, political observers believe Punjab might become the first State to witness a Congress resurgence. https://frontline.thehindu.com/politics/why-aap-lost-delhi-political-failure/article69219062.ece ‘Price of power’ The AAP came to power promising a break from the politics of the Congress, the SAD, and the BJP. But its track record on its poll promises is severely contested. “People had very high expectations of the AAP,” said Jagrup Singh Sekhon, former professor of political science at Guru Nanak Dev University, Amritsar. “They thought the problem of drugs, gangsterism, law and order, unemployment, and mounting fiscal and agrarian crises would be addressed. But the AAP did not live up to those expectations.” Popular discontent has coalesced around the problem of drug addiction. The government campaign on the issue, “Yudh Nasheyan Virudh”, was launched with much fanfare but has not yielded the desired results. The ruling party is perceived to be responsible for the mess. “As we would fight to save our crops, so now we fight to save our generations,” said Sikander Singh. “The AAP promised to end the drug menace. Instead, drugs have become more easily available. Drugs and the AAP have devoured Punjab.” The political damage has also acquired a consequential religious dimension. The acting jathedar of the Akal Takht, the highest temporal authority of Sikhs, has declared Mann “Guru Dokhi” (betrayer of the Guru) and “Khalsa Panth Virodhi” (anti-Khalsa Panth). The State government’s record has also been complicated by the increasingly visceral question of who controls the Punjab’s government. The AAP government has been accused of allowing the ruling party’s central leadership in Delhi to exercise an outsized influence over the State. The impression is that the State’s affairs are being dictated by people with little understanding of, or empathy for, Punjab and its people. Jagtar Singh, a senior journalist based in Punjab, said: “Immediately after the AAP formed the government, the perception in Punjab was that it was being run by people from Delhi. It was an open secret. Punjabis don’t like Delhi dictating the State, but the interference level keeps rising.” The extent of that disconnect became apparent when Bhagwant Mann vacated his Lok Sabha seat after becoming Chief Minister in 2022. Barely three months later, the AAP lost the Sangrur bypoll. “It showed that the party’s connection with the people began to take a hit from the very beginning,” Jagtar Singh said. The AAP, fighting to hold on to its last fort, has attempted to make Mann its Punjab face. Another move has been to drop eight sitting legislators, including Agriculture Minister Gurmeet Singh Khudian, in the party’s second list of candidates for the Assembly election, announced on November 12. But the damage, many observers believe, may be hard to reverse. Sekhon observed: “The damage is already done. Once the Punjab elections are over, I don’t see the AAP continuing as a national party. The AAP may become a marginalised party. That’s the price of power in Punjab.” The revival bid Punjab has five principal contenders heading into next year’s election. Each is fighting, in its own way, to recover the political ground it has lost. The SAD, one of Punjab’s oldest parties, is struggling to reclaim the political space it once occupied almost by default. The Badals’ centralisation of the party weakened its electoral base. Further, its alliance with the BJP—whose centralised model sat uneasily with the SAD’s regional identity—eroded its credibility. By the time the Akalis walked out over the controversial farm laws, they had already ceded much of their Sikh identity or Panthic political space to splinter groups and neo-Panthic forces such as the Akali Dal Waris Punjab De. The SAD was reduced to three Assembly seats in 2022 and one parliamentary seat in 2024. Other groups filled the vacuum with Waris Punjab De chief Amritpal Singh and independent candidate Sarabjeet Singh Khalsa winning two core SAD strongholds, Khadoor Sahib and Faridkot, in 2024. Sarabjeet Singh Khalsa’s father was one of the assassins of former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. Sekhon said: “The BJP has nothing to lose. But if there is any restructuring of the seat-sharing arrangement then the [Shriomani] Akali Dal has a double challenge, and it is already marginalised. People still identify problems [of drugs, corruption, sacrilege, and gangster culture] with its leaders.” He added: “This accumulation of baggage makes the SAD-BJP reunion as much a risk as a political opportunity.” The radical political space also appears to be narrowing. “The era of Amritpal [style of politics] has passed,” Sekhon said. “There was a particular momentum in 2024, especially in rural, agrarian constituencies, where voters wanted to teach Arvind Kejriwal and Narendra Modi a lesson and Amritpal became a vehicle for that anger.” His Akali Dal (Waris Punjab De) later contested the Tarn Taran Assembly bypoll but lost. The BJP has failed to build an independent electoral presence in Punjab, either in seats or in vote share, notwithstanding its 24-year alliance with the SAD. In other States, the BJP has created a record of starting out as a weaker ally to a strong regional party and gradually growing into the dominant force. The did not happen in Punjab. Ashutosh Kumar, professor of political science at Panjab University, Chandigarh, argued in his study “The 2024 Parliamentary Elections and Punjab Politics: Commonalities, Exceptionalism, and Takeaways” (published in the Journal of Sikh & Punjāb Studies in 2024) that the BJP is likely to remain a force in Punjab despite its electoral setbacks. But its growth, he noted, will depend on whether it can move beyond cultural nationalism and religious mobilisation, take clearer positions on issues concerning Punjab and Sikhs, and shed its anti-farmer image. The party also needs stronger State-level leadership, he argued, as its national leaders have little traction in Punjab and leaders brought in from the Congress, including Captain Amarinder Singh, Sunil Jakhar, and Manpreet Badal, have failed to give it the political momentum it needs. The Congress, unlike the SAD and the BJP, is not trying to build a new political base. Notwithstanding its crushing 2022 defeat, the party retained a State-wide organisation and a large social coalition. Its seven Lok Sabha seats in 2024 offered enough evidence that voters who abandoned the party in 2022 had not necessarily moved beyond it. Kumar observed that the Congress has retained a cross-community base that can become electorally decisive if the AAP’s support continues to erode. According to him, the Congress managed to retain its old social base at a time when political loyalties were becoming fragmented in Punjab. Sekhon explained why the Congress has an advantage: “Today, the AAP is no longer the outsider that promised to disrupt Punjab’s established political order. It is the incumbent defending its record. While others are caught in some major crisis or the other, the Congress has returned to being a principal challenger, its most comfortable role in Punjab.” The Congress, meanwhile, has sought to contain factionalism by bringing in Sachin Pilot as Punjab in-charge and former Indian hockey team captain and three-time MLA Pargat Singh as State Congress president. “The combination has helped control the strife to a great extent,” Sekhon said. Harjeshwar Pal Singh, a professor of history, also said that the Congress has a solid base in Punjab. “It has a presence in almost every district, every village, and every mohalla. It has leaders known across the State,” he said. “That is a strength which cannot be created overnight and other parties currently lack it.” The Punjab edge This will be the first State election in northern India since the Cockroach Janata Party(CJP) protests forced the Modi government to confront a series of political controversies. The agitation against the former Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan and then the protests over voter exclusions through the Special Intensive Revision have added to the political goodwill of Rahul Gandhi, as Leader of the Opposition in Parliament, and of the Congress as the major opposition party. Uttar Pradesh, like Punjab, will also go to the polls next year. But in Uttar Pradesh, the Congress remains one among several political players. The BJP, the Samajwadi Party, and the Bahujan Samaj Party all have considerable influence in the Uttar Pradesh contest. Punjab is different. Politics in Uttar Pradesh is influenced by politics at the national level. In contrast, Punjab has remained more immune to national developments. “Punjab has never been swayed by the ‘national constituency phenomenon’, attempted earlier by the Congress and now by the BJP, both polity wide parties,” Professor Ashutosh Kumar wrote in his 2024 study. “The latter’s repeated attempts to contest elections on national issues like national security, Article 370, citizenship, exalted status of India on the global stage, has not cut much ice in the State. On the contrary, even in the Lok Sabha elections, local issues like drugs, mafia hold, the farming sector distress, have remained decisive.” He added: “At a time when there has been a growing perception about a large-scale ideological shift from middle to right-wing conservatism, visible in the ascendance of cultural nationalism in the plains and hills of north, central, and western India, Punjab again seems immune from it, despite having a sizeable Hindu population.” That distinctiveness, in addition to Punjab’s social composition, has created a natural advantage for the Congress. Unlike other political parties, the Congress has usually drawn support across Sikh, Hindu, and Dalit constituencies. “Punjab, along with Kerala, is a State that is most productive for the Congress because it is a catch-all party,” explained Harjeshwar Pal Singh. “It does not cater to one particular social group. It has historically brought different identities into the same political coalition.” No room for complacence The Congress may have emerged as the principal challenger to the AAP, but the voters who want the AAP out still have to decide which party they believe can replace it. This is where this election differs from the 2022 election, as Sekhon explained: “The 2022 election was altogether different. People had an option then that was relatively free of the political record of the established parties. This time, almost all the parties are sailing in the same waters. It’s not a vote for the best party but a choice of lesser evil.” That difference could have implications for the Congress’ prospects. “The biggest advantage of the Congress is that it does not have to convince Punjab to accept it as a political force,” said Harjeshwar Pal Singh. “The question is whether it can convince different social and religious groups that they have a common political interest in bringing the Congress back.” The calculation could also become particularly important among Punjab’s floating voters who have repeatedly shifted their loyalties. “Punjab’s floating voter is not necessarily looking for the party with the strongest ideology,” said Sekhon. “She is looking at which party can actually form the government. Once the voter starts believing that one party has the capacity to win, the floating vote begins moving in that direction.” That is where the Congress’ rise as the principal opposition becomes electorally significant. It makes the party a plausible choice for voters who want to punish the AAP but may not be entirely sure of whom they want to reward, said Sekhon. Yet, there is no room for complacence. “The Congress cannot assume that every voter who is unhappy with the AAP will automatically come to it,” said Jagtar Singh. “Punjab has shown many times that people can reject one party without necessarily choosing the traditional alternative. The Congress has to make itself the obvious alternative. If the voter thinks there is uncertainty about the Congress, the anti-government vote can still be divided.” There is also a limit to what Rahul Gandhi can do for the party. His confrontation with the Modi government and his association with the farmers’ cause have given the Congress an additional political resonance in Punjab. But the Assembly election will eventually be decided on questions of local relevance. “Rahul Gandhi can create a political atmosphere, but the Punjab election will be fought by the State leadership,” said Harjeshwar Pal Singh. “People will ask who is going to run Punjab, what they will do about drugs, employment, farming, and law and order. The Congress has to give them an answer that is bigger than simply defeating the AAP.” Indeed, an anti-incumbency vote many not be easy to consolidate. “People in Punjab defeat a party, they don’t elect a party,” said Jagtar Singh. “They can decide that a government has to go without having already decided which party should replace it.” Zaid Bin Shabir is a journalist based in Srinagar. headline: Why Tamil Nadu’s investment agency is at the centre of an espionage row
content: For more than three decades, Guidance Tamil Nadu has helped politicians announce investments, bureaucrats negotiate with multinational corporations, and professionals build careers in attracting industry. Over the last few weeks, however, its role has come under increased scrutiny as the agency confronts allegations that some of its former professionals helped attract investments to Andhra Pradesh. The departure of 16 employees this year, including three who subsequently joined the Andhra Pradesh Economic Development Board (APEDB), has escalated into accusations of industrial espionage, political disloyalty and the passing of confidential information to a competing state. Guidance has denied reports of mass resignations, and so far there is no established evidence that confidential information was leaked or investments diverted. But the controversy has exposed the problem with blurring the lines between an institution, its political masters and the professionals hired to serve it. Guidance was established in July 1992 as the Tamil Nadu Industrial Guidance and Export Promotion Bureau during J Jayalalithaa’s first government. Its purpose was simple: to give investors a single point of contact instead of requiring them to navigate several departments independently. Under successive administrations led by M Karunanidhi, Jayalalithaa, Edappadi K Palaniswami and M K Stalin, it developed into a professional agency, with IAS officers providing administrative leadership and consultants handling investor outreach, negotiations and project coordination. Consultants could initiate conversations, identify opportunities and help companies navigate approvals. But investment decisions passed through senior bureaucrats, the Industries Department and, where necessary, the Cabinet. That distinction matters because Tamil Nadu’s industrial strength rests on something considerably larger than the relationships cultivated by individual consultants. According to the state’s Economic Survey 2025–26, Tamil Nadu accounted for 15.4 per cent of India’s registered factories in 2023–24, compared with Gujarat’s 12.8 per cent, Maharashtra’s 10.2 per cent and Andhra Pradesh’s 6.2 per cent. The state had 1,735 factories employing at least 1,000 people each, against 742 in Maharashtra and 679 in Gujarat. It also had 311 factories employing 5,000 or more workers, accounting for 35 per cent of India’s total, compared with Gujarat’s 66. Tamil Nadu accounted for 15.2 per cent of factory employment and ranked third in manufacturing gross value added. Manufacturing contributed 24.5 per cent of the state’s gross value added in 2024–25, against the national average of 17.2 per cent. These figures reflect decades of industrial development, with ports, highways, suppliers, engineering institutions and skilled workers supporting one another. From resignations to espionage claims The controversy emerged after the TVK government assumed office in May. According to people familiar with the departures, 15 Guidance employees left in 2025 and 16 in 2026. Five of this year’s departures had already resigned or were serving notice before the change of government. Eleven left between May and July, including at least three who cited personal circumstances. A senior source in the TVK government told The Indian Express that at least two consultants were asked to resign within weeks of the new administration taking office. “It is true that one of them was asked to quit immediately,” the source said. The other case, the source said, created considerable anxiety within the government. A consultant was suspected of suggesting to a foreign company, after TVK assumed power, that it consider investing in Andhra Pradesh instead. “This had panicked the new government, forcing them to travel to an East Asian country to ensure that there was no impact due to this,” the source said. Three former Guidance professionals subsequently joined Andhra Pradesh’s investment promotion apparatus and participated in activities including the CII Partnership Summit in Visakhapatnam, where investment commitments approaching Rs 10 lakh crore were announced. Their employment with a competing state agency became central to suggestions that commercially sensitive information had travelled across state borders. On Friday, Guidance rejected reports of mass resignations in July, describing departures as normal organisational attrition arising from career opportunities, higher education, relocation and family circumstances. It also emphasised constructive competition between states. However, an examination of the circumstances surrounding more than a dozen departures suggests a combination of political mistrust, administrative restructuring, workplace tensions and ordinary professional mobility. According to people familiar with the transition, the new TVK administration was uneasy about the proximity of certain senior consultants to the previous DMK leadership. The change of government also brought changes in Guidance’s leadership. Sources familiar with Guidance’s functioning said that of the 16 employees who left in 2026, five had already resigned or were serving notice before the TVK government assumed office, while at least three of the subsequent departures involved personal circumstances, including family relocation. Two senior professionals were asked to leave abruptly at the end of June. One senior consultant, who had a close association with the previous government, secured a better-paid position with a Taiwanese multinational. The transition also generated complaints within the organisation. An outgoing employee wrote to the Chief Minister’s Office and senior officials at the end of July, alleging a hostile working environment, threats and preferential treatment under the new management. Multiple sources aware of the incident spoke of fear and anxiety over the loyalty of professionals that made the leadership hostile. “Unlike the DMK and AIADMK, TVK entered government without an earlier administrative record, making inherited relationships within sensitive agencies a source not only of suspicion but also of fear,” said a top government source aware of the development. Political backlash The dispute has drawn criticism from both principal Opposition parties. AIADMK general secretary Edappadi K Palaniswami pointed out that several professionals had been recruited under his administration and accused the TVK government of undermining an institution established during Jayalalithaa’s tenure. Former industries minister T R B Rajaa argued that the DMK had retained professionals appointed by the AIADMK because institutional experience mattered. Former finance minister P T R Palanivel Thiaga Rajan questioned how contractual employees without final decision-making authority could determine the investment fortunes of an entire state when proposals passed through multiple administrative and political levels. A former industries secretary explained what investors actually consider before committing to a state. “Companies negotiating major investments routinely compare several states and countries. They examine land prices, power availability, logistics, fiscal incentives, suppliers, skilled labour and the reliability of government approvals. Investment professionals can influence negotiations and may possess commercially sensitive information. But companies themselves frequently disclose competing incentive packages while seeking better offers. Knowledge of those proposals does not, by itself, establish espionage,” the ex-secretary said. A principal secretary in the Tamil Nadu government told The Indian Express that the larger concern, for Tamil Nadu, may be uncertainty during a political transition. “Investors usually wait when there is a regime change. Multinational companies making commitments that will mature over decades want assurances that approvals, land allotments and incentives negotiated under one government will survive the next,” he said, adding that the challenge was particularly important for TVK, which was governing the state for the first time. The principal secretary also pointed to Andhra Pradesh’s emphasis on policy continuity. On November 12, Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu announced plans for an Investment Protection Act intended to safeguard government commitments involving land, incentives and approvals against future political changes. The state has also proposed an escrow mechanism to support timely payment of industrial incentives. “The legislation has not been enacted, and its effectiveness remains untested. But the proposal addresses a familiar concern among investors: that an electoral change can also change the terms of a long-term investment. Andhra Pradesh’s announced investments remain commitments, not operational factories. Tamil Nadu’s established manufacturing base cannot be replicated merely by offering incentives or recruiting experienced professionals. What can be affected more quickly is confidence in the institutions responsible for negotiating and implementing those commitments. That is the larger significance of the Guidance controversy,” he said. The former industries secretary added, “A politician or a party can seek another mandate and rebuild credibility through another campaign. An institution cannot. Its credibility is harder to recover – and, in the business of attracting factories, considerably more expensive to lose."

headline: J-K doctors protest enters 6th day; Health Minister assures priority examination of stipend demand
content: Amid the ongoing protest by postgraduate (PG) and senior resident doctors, Jammu and Kashmir Health Minister Sakina Itoo on Monday met the protesting doctors and assured them that their demand for a stipend hike would be “examined on priority”.The protesting doctors are demanding an increase in stipends and parity with their counterparts in other states and Union Territories.Itoo met the protesting PG and senior resident doctors at GMC Srinagar and assured them that their demand would be examined on priority. She also urged them to “resume duties to ensure patient care is not affected”.However, despite the minister’s assurance, the All India Medical Students’ Association (AIMSA) said on Monday that the agitation would continue.The doctors’ body said the protests had also spread from medical colleges to several district hospitals across Jammu and Kashmir.The protest on Monday entered its fifth day at GMC Srinagar and its sixth day at GMC Jammu.The association said that during their interaction with the minister, doctors had highlighted the disparity in stipends “compared to their counterparts elsewhere in the country” and sought appropriate maternity leave provisions.The minister assured them that their concerns would be examined.AIMSA also said the protest had “gained further momentum as doctors at several district hospitals announced peaceful protests in solidarity”.On Monday, Peoples Democratic Party leader Iltija Mufti also visited GMC Srinagar, where she interacted with the protesting PG residents and listened to their concerns.“Support from leaders across political parties was welcome, stressing that the movement was focused on the legitimate demands and welfare of resident doctors and would remain peaceful and democratic,” AIMSA said.Mohammad Momin Khan, president of AIMSA J-K, welcomed Itoo’s interaction with the protesting PG residents and expressed hope that the minister would take concrete steps to fulfil the genuine demands of PG and senior resident doctors and “ensure an early resolution, as the government had done in the case of MBBS and BDS interns”.Last week, a series of circulars and notices were issued by various medical institutions, warning resident doctors against disrupting academic activities and patient-care services through protests.

headline: Zambia opposition leader charged with attempting to overthrow government
content: By Chris MfulaLUSAKA, Nov 23 (Reuters) – Zambian opposition leader Brian Mundubile and more than a dozen associates have been charged with trying to overthrow the government and committed to the High Court to stand trial for treason, according to a charge sheet read in court on Monday. • Mundubile and his running mate, Makebi Zulu, were arrested and questioned over alleged treason shortly after the August 13 presidential election, which they claimed was rigged • President Hakainde Hichilema won reelection and denied the fraud allegations • Mundubile, Zulu and 12 others have been charged with plotting to overthrow the government between April and August 2026, according to the charge sheet • The charge sheet said that Mundubile and a businessman had provided financial resources for military training in Russia for five people for the purpose of trying to overthrow the government • A lawyer for the defence, Sakwiba Sikota, said the charges did not make sense and that the prosecution was on a “fishing expedition”

headline: Agra’s Emotional Education Work Earns a Global Platform in Manila
content: PNN New Delhi [India], November 23: Psychologist Dr. Chinu Agrawal presented India’s emotional education efforts at the Second Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children in Manila, held on 18 and 19 November. She attended at the invitation of the World Health Organization (WHO) and UNICEF. The conference brought together ministers, policymakers, UN representatives and child protection experts. Discussions focused on preventing violence from the outset rather than acting after an incident, including helping children become emotionally aware and capable. * Dr. Chinu Agrawal presents India’s approach at WHO-UNICEF conference * Protecting children from violence now depends on their emotional strength as well as on laws and safety systems. An initiative that began in Agra has won a place on the international stage. Governments from 94 countries announced 283 commitments, covering safe homes and schools, the role of parents, mental health and stronger child protection systems. A decade of work Dr. Dr. Agarwal is the founder and director of Feeling Minds and founding president of the International Society for Mental Health Advocacy and Action (ISMHAA). In Manila she spoke about the organisation’s work since 2016, India’s first Emotional Education Lab and the E-Cube experiential learning model. Feeling Minds aims to make emotional education a regular part of schooling. Students learn to recognise their feelings, manage anger and stress, understand others, communicate, resolve disputes and build healthy relationships. Through its FEEL-SEAL programme and the E-Cube lab, activities and hands-on experiences make psychology practical for children. The organisation says it has reached over 4 lakh students and trained more than 2,500 teachers. Conversations in Manila Dr. Agrawal discussed school-based emotional education and her working model with delegates and experts from several countries. She met United Nations Assistant Secretary-General and UNICEF Deputy Executive Director. Mr. Ted Chaiban; Dr. Daniela Ligiero, CEO of Together for Girls and the Brave Movement; and Dr. Sabine Rakotomalala, Technical Officer in WHO’s violence prevention unit. She also spoke with Philippine Cabinet Secretary Benjamin Abalos Jr., Health Secretary Dr. Edwin Mercado, Secretary of Health, Government of the Philippines, Atty. Raul T. Vasquez, Undersecretary, Department of Justice, Government of the Philippines; Nepali parliamentarian Ms.Prabha Dhakal and Hon. Ada Maria Mejia Signorelli, Honduras’ State Minister for Children, Adolescents and Family Affairs, and exchanged views with officials of the Indian delegation. From the Indian delegation, she exchanged views with Dr. Govind Kumar Bansal, Director, Maternal Health, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India, and Dr. Rachana Kathuria, National Professional Officer, Adolescent Health, WHO India, among other officials. The conference noted that teaching children to spot unsafe situations, speak up about their troubles, seek help and understand their boundaries is a key part of prevention. Emotional education builds these abilities. It does not replace laws, safety systems or professional mental health services, but strengthens them. “India has a lot to offer the world,” said Dr. Agrawal, calling it an important opportunity to share the country’s efforts at the invitation of WHO and UNICEF. Keeping children safe, she said, requires safe homes, supportive schools, aware parents and emotionally intelligent communities. Telling children what is right and wrong is not enough, because they must also learn to understand their feelings and needs. International delegates showed interest in the Feeling Minds model and the E-Cube lab in Agra. The talks also touched on knowledge exchange and possible collaboration, and on ISMHAA’s proposed Youth Mental Wellbeing Summit in Agra. For Agra, the recognition carries particular weight: an effort that started in schools in 2016 is now part of the global conversation on child protection. About Feeling Minds Founded in 2016 and based in Agra, Feeling Minds works in psychology, emotional education and mental health, running experience-based training programmes for children, parents, teachers and professionals. Beyond the lab, FEEL-SEAL and E-Cube, its initiatives include school mental health programmes, teacher capacity building, parent education and professional training. headline: Booze on tap: Liquor ‘flows’ from handpump in UP’s Jhansi village, woman arrested
content: In a village in Uttar Pradesh's Jhansi district, handpumps did more than draw water -- they were used by villagers to allegedly dispense illicit country-made liquor stored in underground tanks, police said on Monday. The operation came to light during a raid at Kabutra Dera in the Sakrar police station area as part of a special drive against illegal country-made liquor manufacturing and sale in the district, they said.Police, in coordination with the excise department, seized more than 1,000 litres of 'lahan' (fermented liquid used to make country liquor) from the premises two days ago and destroyed it in the presence of competent officials.A woman, identified as Vinita, wife of Raman Kabutra and a resident of Tejpur Ghurat, was also arrested with 30 litres of illicit country-made liquor, police said."The accused allegedly manufactured illicit liquor and stored it in underground tanks. They subsequently used pipes connected to handpumps to draw out the liquor and sell it, with male accomplices keeping watch," Sakrar Station House Officer Pappu Singh said."Police are now searching for other locations allegedly used by those involved in the illegal trade," he added.
