headline: The Cockroach Club is going national. What CJP wants to build
content: On a stage at Gandhi Bhavan in Kothrud on Friday, a performer played Mahatma Gandhi and put him face to face with the political realities of present-day India. Around 250 people watched: activists, comedians, digital creators and volunteers of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP). The three-hour programme, "Legacy of Bapu," was the first outing of the "Cockroach Club." The CJP, which built its following by using satire to question politics, hopes the club will take it beyond cities and into districts and villages. The launch of the club comes a week after CJP named zonal members to work on the ground in 10 states. The CJP says its membership has crossed 15 lakh, though a senior member acknowledged the figure still needs to be verified. On November 14, the CJP named zonal leaders and set up coordination committees covering 10 zones, including Uttar Pradesh, where Assembly elections are ahead. The group says the timing is coincidental. Ajinkya Shinde, its national organisation in-charge, said the committees would start with Lok Sabha constituencies and move to Assembly seats as membership grows, with the aim of holding elected representatives accountable. An Experiment The evening ran on an open-stage format, with satire, poetry, music and debate used to take up political and civic questions.. Ashutosh Ranka, a senior CJP member, said the aim was to give young people a place to think about where India has been and where it is going. "The idea behind this initiative is to create a space that gives young people exactly that opportunity," Ranka said. "We discuss what defines the Cockroach Janata Party, what our ideology is, and the contributions of people such as Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru and B R Ambedkar." Ranka said that the club is a work in progress. Over the next few months, he said the group will try out formats in different cities, which could include film screenings, lectures, book readings, debates and cultural performances. It will then settle on a model to replicate nationwide, he said. "We are still in an experimental phase, trying to understand what works, what kind of model is sustainable and what resonates with the public and our supporters," he said. Ranka said that funding is informal and the group is relying on community participation and crowdfunding, and at the Pune event a donation box was placed at the venue. "It has to become a collective effort," Ranka said. Asked whether the club would also go to states not governed by the BJP, Ranka said it would not be bound by political lines. The group is planning what he called a listening tour, with visits to Patna, Ranchi, Bengaluru, Rajasthan, Delhi and Varanasi, among other places. "Our ideology is the Constitution" On ideology, Ranka said the CJP draws on Gandhi, Nehru and Ambedkar but treats the Constitution as its central guide. He described it as a document drafted by people from across the spectrum, from socialists to capitalists and from the extreme Left to the extreme Right. "That is precisely what we want our ideology to reflect," he said. “Setting up the club is not a step toward launching a party and the aim is to bring about deeper social and political change rather than stop at protests or calls for resignations,” he said. "We are very effective as an independent pressure group and we are going to continue with that," Ranka said. The CJP was formed in May this year after Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant compared some youths to cockroaches. Following the remark, Abhijeet Dipke, a 30-year-old from Maharashtra who was studying in Boston, created an Instagram account named Cockroach Janta Party (CJP). The account reportedly attracted two crore followers within a day. Dipke subsequently joined hands with two friends, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, in India to organise a protest against the NEET paper leak in June-July. Thousands gathered at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi in support of the demonstration, which demanded the resignation of then Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

headline: Quality education a priority in Himachal: Rajesh Dharmani
content: Technical Education Minister Rajesh Dharmani said providing quality education and better opportunities to students was a top priority of the state government. He was addressing students at the annual function of Government Senior Secondary School in Marhana village of Bilaspur district today.He said the government was working to equip government schools with modern facilities and provide a better academic environment to ensure that students in rural areas had equal access to quality education. The government was establishing Rajiv Gandhi Model Day-Boarding Schools and developing more than 850 educational institutions as Institutions of Excellence, with a special focus on providing modern academic facilities.Dharmani said that, to address teacher shortages and improve the quality of education, the government was focusing not only on regular recruitment but also on comprehensive teacher training. He added that teachers had been sent on exposure visits to countries such as Singapore to gain first-hand experience of modern teaching methods.Additionally, the Vidya Samiksha Kendra was being used to monitor academic activities in schools in real time and ensure the optimum utilisation of available resources. The minister announced a grant of Rs 5 lakh for various development works and improving student facilities at the school.Speaking about development works in the village, Dharmani said more than Rs 40 lakh had been spent on the maintenance and improvement of roads in Marhana panchayat through the Public Works Department (PWD). The works included the construction of retaining walls at various locations, installation of paver blocks in vulnerable areas and construction of drainage systems along most stretches of the road. Repair work on the road connecting the village had also been completed.He said around Rs 7.50 lakh was being spent on the renovation and improvement of the Marhana dispensary building. Another Rs 10 lakh had been sanctioned to the PWD under the Mukhyamantri Gram Sadak Yojana to improve the access road to the Dalit settlement in Marhana.

headline: Congress revokes suspension of former Ghanaur MLA Madan Lal Jalalpur
content: The Congress has revoked the suspension of former Ghanaur MLA Madan Lal Jalalpur.In August, Jalalpur was suspended from the party during the tenure of Amarinder Singh Raja Warring. Party insiders said Jalalpur and his son, Gagandeep, had recently met PPCC chief Pargat Singh, who reportedly assured them that the suspension would be revoked.Former chief minister Charanjit Channi, who had backed Jalalpur, is also believed to have played a key role in securing the revocation.The Congress high command's decision is being viewed as more than a routine disciplinary reversal. It comes amid concerted efforts to prevent factional battles within the Punjab Congress from spilling over in the run-up to the 2027 Assembly election.After former Rajpura MLA Hardyal Kamboj switched from the Congress to the BJP, Jalalpur had started flexing his political muscle. Recently, he alleged that the PPCC was being run by confidants of Warring.Reacting to Jalalpur's statement, Warring said he had no say in the functioning of the PPCC after he relinquished the charge.Jalalpur was suspended from the party over his remarks criticising senior central leaders, including KC Venugopal and Bhupesh Baghel, for retaining Warring as Punjab Congress chief before he was replaced.He had also alleged that the party did not try to prevent Kamboj from leaving. He had also expressed displeasure over the fact that none of the leaders from the Patiala parliamentary constituency had been consulted regarding the municipal elections in Patiala.

headline: ‘Power panel left open for months’: Mother of 11-yr-old boy electrocuted in Delhi
content: Two days after an 11-year-old boy died in West Delhi’s Vikaspuri after allegedly suffering an electric shock inside a feeder pillar where he was playing, the victim’s mother alleged that the electrical panel was left open for months. “It was a public place. A whole market is there. It (the electrical panel) was left open for months. The wires were then covered with wooden planks,” said Riya Singh, Ashish’s mother. “Ashish left the house at about 4 pm on Friday, and was playing hide-and-seek. He would never go near the voltage box. But what will a child do when wires are lying everywhere,” she said. While an FIR has been filed under relevant sections of negligence, electricity supplier BSES had said that the cover of the electricity feeder had allegedly been stolen and no complaint was registered. In a statement, BSES had said, “Our condolences are with the family of the deceased. As per preliminary information, the child, a resident of a nearby JJ cluster, was reportedly playing when he entered an electricity feeder pillar in Vikaspuri to hide. The cover of the feeder pillar had reportedly been stolen for which the discom had no intimation or complaint. BSES is fully cooperating with the Delhi Police in their investigation to ascertain the circumstances surrounding the incident. Our officials are also in touch with the bereaved family to extend necessary assistance and facilitate compensation as applicable under the relevant provisions.” It added, “BSES once again appeals to residents to maintain a safe distance from electrical installations, including feeder pillars, transformers, substations and electricity poles. Parents and guardians are particularly urged to ensure that children do not play near or enter electrical installations. Residents are also requested to immediately report any open, damaged or tampered electrical installations to BSES." Delhi has seen several such incidents in recent times when children have become victims in similar manner in public spaces while playing. In May 2025, a nine-year-old boy was electrocuted while playing at an MCD park in South Delhi’s Kalkaji, reportedly after coming in contact with an open switchboard near an electrical pole. In August 2024, a 13-year-old boy died after allegedly coming in contact with an electric pole while playing cricket at a ground in West Delhi’s Ranhola. The pole was reportedly supplying electricity to a nearby cowshed.

headline: Phone & WhatsApp numbers, QR code: BJP seeks suggestions for 2027 poll manifesto
content: With the 2027 Punjab Assembly elections drawing closer, the BJP has launched a statewide public outreach exercise to seek suggestions from different sections of society for its poll manifesto, or 'Sankalp Patra', setting a mid-December deadline for completing consultations. As part of the exercise, the party on Sunday released three contact numbers and a QR code to invite suggestions directly from people. The numbers are 07971943333 (direct phone call, with “0” prefix mandatory), 9913002027 (missed call, following which the party team will call back) and 71508560065 (WhatsApp). BJP state president Kewal Singh Dhillon said, “The exercise has begun, and people can share their suggestions through these channels. Our campaign vans will also travel across Punjab, carrying information about various central government schemes. The contact numbers will be displayed on these vans, which will also have suggestion boxes for people to submit their inputs.” The manifesto exercise began in Chandigarh on Thursday evening, with a meeting with intellectuals, where the party sought their views on Punjab's pressing challenges, people's expectations and the roadmap for the state's development. A 13-member manifesto committee was constituted on November 15 under the chairmanship of former BJP state president Avinash Rai Khanna. Six members of the committee will directly interact with people, while the remaining members will be involved in screening suggestions and drafting the document. “Six members, including I, will collect feedback from industry representatives, traders, farmers, women, youngsters, employees, pensioners and other sections of society. Each member will be assigned four districts,” Khanna told The Indian Express. The screening committee would be headed by BJP national vice-president Manpreet Singh Badal, Dhillon said. Khanna said the party wanted the manifesto to reflect the expectations and aspirations of people across Punjab rather than limiting the exercise to consultations within the organisation. He cited the example of Sewa Kendra employees, with whom the committee had already interacted during the first round of consultations. “It is painful to know that 2,600 employees working in these kendras, which generate revenue of not less than Rs 100 crore annually, are outsourced and receive a monthly salary of just Rs 12,700,” he said. Asked whether the BJP would announce freebies or welfare measures in its manifesto, Dhillon said existing welfare schemes would continue, with an emphasis on improving their delivery. He also indicated that revenue generation would be an important focus. “The BJP is running various welfare schemes across the country and in other BJP-ruled states. These schemes will continue in Punjab and their delivery will be streamlined. At the same time, we will focus on generating revenue, unlike the ruling AAP, which has pushed the state into heavy debt,” he said. The other members of the manifesto committee are Manpreet Singh Badal, Ashwani Sharma, Manoranjan Kalia, Som Parkash, Rana Gurmeet Singh Sodhi, Ashwani Sekhri, Satnam Singh Sandhu, Raghav Chadha, Rajinder Gupta, Harbhajan Singh, Parampal Kaur and advocate HS. Phoolka. Barring Chadha, Satnam Singh Sandhu and Harbhajan Singh, all other members were present on Sunday. On pre-poll alliance Asked about the possibility of an alliance ahead of the 2027 Assembly elections, Dhillon said, “As of now, we are preparing for all 117 seats. Otherwise, we will abide by the directions of the high command, whatever it decides.” He had earlier said that the BJP would contest the polls on its own. Asked whether any alliance announcement could be expected at the December 8 rally being organised by the SAD in Moga to mark the birth anniversary of former chief minister Parkash Singh Badal, Dhillon said the BJP had received no information about any such alliance. Ruling out the AAP as a political challenge, he said the BJP is a national party with governments in more than 20 states and at the Centre. “We are a larger party and the AAP is going to be routed from Punjab as well. A double-engine government is the only solution for Punjab,” he added.

headline: Is Your Bisleri Water Safe To Drink? What The Latest FSSAI Action Means
content: For many Indians, bottled water is one of those things bought without a second thought. The familiar green bottle at an airport, railway station, restaurant or roadside shop is often the easiest way to ensure access to drinking water. But a recent food safety finding involving Bisleri has put that everyday habit under scrutiny. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd after a sample of its packaged drinking water was declared unsafe in laboratory testing. The sample reportedly failed to meet prescribed bromate limits. Following an appeal by the company, a referral laboratory also declared it unsafe after detecting polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). What Is Bromate, And Why Is It A Concern? Bromate is a chemical that can form during water treatment, particularly when ozone is used for disinfection. Ozone helps eliminate microorganisms, but it can react with bromide naturally present in water and produce bromate. This is why the treatment process needs to be carefully controlled. The concern is that bromate exposure over time may increase cancer risk. The World Health Organization (WHO) has set a provisional guideline value of 10 micrograms per litre for bromate in drinking water. The guideline is based on toxicological evidence, including animal studies that found tumours in the kidneys, thyroid and other tissues. Bromate is also difficult to remove once it forms, making prevention and monitoring during the water-treatment process particularly important. Its presence is not something consumers can identify by looking at a bottle or tasting the water. A regulatory sample of "Packaged Drinking Water (other than Mineral Water)" was collected from the premises of M/s Bisleri International Pvt. Ltd. for analysis. The sample was found non-compliant with the prescribed bromate limits and declared unsafe under the FSS Act, 2006. Upon appeal by the FBO, the sample was referred to the Referral Food Laboratory, which also declared it unsafe due to the detection of polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). The laboratory findings established violations relating to unsafe food under the FSS Act, 2006. Sanction has been granted to launch prosecution under the FSS Act, 2006, against M/s Bisleri International Pvt. Ltd @fssaiindia — DD News (@DDNewslive) November 22, 2026 What Are PAHs, And How Can They Enter Drinking Water? The second finding in the Bisleri sample involved polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons, commonly referred to as PAHs. These are a group of chemicals that can form when organic material burns incompletely. They can also be found in coal, petroleum, vehicle emissions, industrial pollution and smoke. Not all PAHs carry the same health risks, but some are known carcinogens. Benzo[a]pyrene, for instance, is associated with cancer risk and has a WHO drinking-water guideline value of 0.7 micrograms per litre. Certain PAHs can be processed by the body into compounds that interact with DNA, potentially causing cellular damage. PAHs can enter drinking water through environmental contamination or contact with certain materials used in water storage and distribution. As per WHO, coal-tar-based coatings in deteriorating water pipes can be a source of PAH contamination. How Did The Contaminants Enter The Water? The findings raise questions about where contamination could have occurred. Potential sources include the water used during production, treatment-related chemical reactions, environmental contamination or contact with materials used in storage and packaging. Bromate, in particular, can form during ozonation, which makes monitoring treatment conditions an important part of water safety. The Bisleri case also comes at a time when packaged drinking water quality has been under regulatory scrutiny. Government data presented in Parliament showed that 333 of 1,300 enforcement samples tested in 2023–24 did not conform to prescribed standards. In 2022–23, 650 of 1,776 samples were found non-conforming. These figures point to a wider compliance concern within the packaged-water sector, rather than an issue that can be viewed only through one brand. Reuters reported that Bisleri said a sample from its Goa facility tested last year contained 12 micrograms per litre of bromate, against the 10-microgram limit. The company also said independent testing it arranged later found bromate levels within limits, and that it would cooperate with the regulator. Can Consumers Identify Unsafe Bottled Water? Not always. Chemical contaminants such as bromate and PAHs cannot reliably be detected through the colour, smell or taste of water. A bottle may appear perfectly clear and still require laboratory testing to establish its chemical safety. Consumers can, however, take some basic precautions: – Check the FSSAI licence details, batch number and packaging or best-before information. – Make sure the cap and seal are intact before opening. – Avoid bottles that are leaking, damaged or visibly contaminated. – Buy from retailers who store bottled water away from direct sunlight and excessive heat. – Avoid drinking from bottles that have been tampered with or improperly stored.

headline: Imran Khan May Face Irreversible Heart Damage, 'Serious' Health Consequences 'Within Days', Warns Doctor
content: Pakistan’s jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan must be examined by a medical specialist within days to prevent potentially irreversible damage to his heart and other vital organs, his personal physician has warned, amid growing concerns over his deteriorating health in prison. Dr Faisal Sultan, who has been treating Khan for more than 30 years, has urged Pakistani authorities to immediately allow the former Prime Minister to consult a specialist, warning that his persistently high blood pressure could have serious consequences if left untreated. Speaking to The Telegraph, Sultan said Khan needed to be examined by a nephrologist or cardiologist without delay. “If I had a patient who had this kind of high blood pressure reading, I’d get them to see a good nephrologist or cardiologist as soon as possible, today or tomorrow. The blood pressure needs to be brought down within days,” he was quoted as saying. Khan, 74, has been lodged in Rawalpindi’s Adiala jail since August 2023 following his arrest in corruption cases, which he denies. His personal doctor warned that prolonged hypertension could affect several major organs, including the heart, kidneys and eyes. “In reality, sustained hypertension risks impacting kidney function and the heart itself. The heart has to strain against a higher pressure,” Sultan said, adding that the retina could also be affected by persistently elevated blood pressure. IMRAN KHAN WARNS HE MAY NOT RETURN ALIVE FROM JAIL The medical warning comes days after Khan appealed to Pakistan’s top judicial authorities for urgent intervention, claiming that his health and that of his wife, Bushra Bibi, were deteriorating and that earlier court directions concerning their medical treatment had not been implemented. In an open letter made public on November 16, Khan said his condition had reached a point where he feared he might not survive without immediate medical attention. “At seventy-four, this unrelenting state is taking me to a place from which I may not return alive,” he wrote. According to Reuters, Khan said doctors had warned him that he was highly vulnerable to a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest. He also claimed that his blood pressure had reached 192 and 193 on November 10. In the letter, Khan alleged that prolonged solitary confinement and inadequate access to medical care had contributed to his deteriorating condition. He said he had been kept isolated for up to 22 hours a day since December 20, 2025. CLAIMS 85% VISION LOSS IN RIGHT EYE Khan also claimed in his letter that he had lost 85 per cent of the vision in his right eye, raising concerns about the medical attention he has received in prison. His personal physician was quoted by the report as saying that the consequences of prolonged high blood pressure could extend beyond immediate symptoms and cause lasting damage. “Having a heart that strains against high blood pressure leads to hypertrophy of the heart muscle,” Sultan said. He stressed the importance of controlling blood pressure before serious organ damage occurs, adding, “It is very important to correct and fix blood pressure readings in time so that no serious injuries are sustained by these organs.” Sultan also suggested that Khan’s prolonged isolation could be contributing to his health problems. “Social isolation certainly may be contributing to this blood pressure problem,” he said, adding, “Without a doubt, I would like to see him.” SUPREME COURT ORDER ON MEDICAL TREATMENT The issue of Khan’s medical treatment had earlier reached Pakistan’s Supreme Court. On August 18, the court directed authorities to move him to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad for an independent medical assessment. According to news agency PTI, the court had ordered that Khan be shifted to the hospital within two days, that a medical board be constituted to examine him and that he be allowed regular contact with his family. The directions also included weekly meetings with family members and telephone conversations with his sons twice a week. However, Khan’s supporters have alleged that these directions were not implemented. Although authorities took him to a hospital for an eye examination last week, Reuters reported that he was subsequently returned to his prison cell. Sultan had reportedly waited at the hospital to examine Khan after the Supreme Court’s order. However, the former Prime Minister was instead taken to a government hospital, where doctors concluded that he was fit to return to jail. WIFE BUSHRA BIBI’S HEALTH ALSO A CONCERN Khan has also raised concerns about the health of his wife, Bushra Bibi, who is imprisoned in a separate case. In his letter, he alleged that she was suffering from deteriorating eyesight and could face permanent vision loss without further medical intervention. Bushra Bibi had suffered a retinal detachment in April and undergone surgery. Khan claimed that she was subsequently returned to solitary confinement and denied access to her doctors and medical records. He said that when he met her on November 11, she could neither tolerate light nor open her eyes. The former Prime Minister also alleged that prison authorities had denied him regular meetings with his wife and prevented his sons, Kasim and Sulaiman, from speaking to him despite court orders. According to PTI, Khan claimed that a jail medical board had recorded his anxiety and recommended more frequent contact with his family, along with access to books and television. He alleged that these recommendations had not been implemented.

headline: Supreme Court panel pulls up 3 states over illegal sand mining in Chambal Sanctuary
content: The Supreme Court-constituted Central Empowered Committee (CEC) has flagged gaps in enforcement measures reported by Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh to curb illegal sand mining in the National Chambal Sanctuary, highlighting manpower shortages, incomplete surveillance infrastructure, discrepancies in enforcement data and lapses in vehicle confiscation procedures.In its report submitted to the Supreme Court, the CEC specifically directed Uttar Pradesh to immediately fill the vacant posts of Deputy Conservator of Forests (DCF) and Assistant Conservator of Forests (ACF) at the National Chambal Wildlife Sanctuary, Agra, noting that both positions had remained vacant for months.While the DCF's additional charge had been assigned to the Divisional Forest Officer, Agra, no officer had been assigned charge of the ACF post, the committee observed. It asked all three states to ensure that sensitive and important forest positions do not remain vacant for prolonged periods and that arrangements are made for timely filling of posts in the event of future vacancies.Madhya Pradesh, meanwhile, reported 211 personnel against 223 sanctioned forest staff posts, leaving 12 vacancies, including nine Deputy Range Officer and two Range Officer posts. The CEC said that manpower requirements needed to be assessed in view of the area requiring patrolling, vulnerable river stretches and the need for round-the-clock enforcement.It reported installation of 42 CCTV cameras at 18 locations, 30 body cameras, 12 dash cameras in six vehicles, an AI surveillance system and four operational control rooms. However, the wireless communication system was still at the tender stage and all 16 permanent check-posts had not been completed. The state reported that 1,250 vehicles had been impounded — 682 in Morena, 165 in Sheopur and 403 in Bhind — but the committee sought complete and reconciled information on confiscation and GPS monitoring, including district-wise enforcement outcomes.In Rajasthan's Dholpur, the CEC expressed concern over vehicles impounded in illegal sand mining and forest offence cases reportedly being released while confiscation proceedings were pending. It asked the state to submit vehicle-wise details and examine whether statutory procedures had been followed.The report also raised concerns over inter-state coordination, urging Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh to share information on offenders, vehicle seizures, confiscation proceedings, routes, prosecutions and penalties through a common reporting mechanism until an integrated dashboard becomes operational.On illegal sand mining allegations along the Ken river, the CEC found discrepancies in enforcement figures furnished by the Forest Department and Mineral Branch, as well as inconsistencies within the Mineral Branch's own records.

headline: Teacher ‘assaulted with sticks’ as his scooter runs over businessman’s leg in Barabanki
content: A 45-year-old private teacher was allegedly assaulted on a road in Barabanki's Kotwali area on Saturday after his scooter allegedly ran over the leg of a 30-year-old businessman. A purported video of the incident has since gone viral. Based on a complaint filed by victim Mohammad Afzal, police have lodged a case against one Babloo Thakur under BNS Sections 115 (voluntarily causing hurt), 352 (intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of peace), 351 (criminal intimidation) and 324 (mischief). “The police have also booked Babloo Thakur for breach of peace,” said Barabanki Additional Superintendent of Police Mohammad Aftab Alam. He added that during the investigation, it emerged that one of the scooter's tyres had run over Thakur's foot, triggering the altercation. According to police, Mohammad Afzal, a resident of Krishna Nagar locality, stated in his complaint that he was travelling on his scooter at around 1.30 pm on Friday when Thakur, who owns a shop, suddenly came in front of his vehicle near Kamariya Bagh crossing. Afzal managed to apply the brakes and stop the scooter to avoid hitting him. However, Afzal alleged that Thakur began abusing him and assaulted him, first with his hands and then with a stick, repeatedly striking him on the head. When he tried to shield himself and fend off the blows with his hand, he sustained a fracture. Afzal further alleged that after assaulting him and leaving him seriously injured, Thakur pelted his scooter with bricks, causing extensive damage. He also repeatedly threatened to kill him during the assault, Afzal alleged. The matter was resolved when the police reached the spot. Afzal said the incident could be verified through CCTV footage and statements of local residents and shopkeepers.

headline: When Yogi Adityanath sought alms from his mother after becoming monk
content: Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath on Monday recalled an emotional encounter with his mother after embracing his monastic life, narrating how he sought alms from her in saffron robes and how she struggled to come to terms with his decision.In the latest edition of his ongoing series of open letters, 'Yogi Ki Paati', Adityanath described a mother's love as "the most beautiful emotion" and said her absence meant "not just the loss of a person but also of emotional security, unconditional love and the deep shade of a home."Recalling his visit to his ancestral village Panchur in Uttarakhand more than three years after becoming a monk, he said he had stood outside his home in saffron robes and sought alms as part of an important ritual of the monastic tradition."When my mother came outside after hearing my voice, she could hardly believe it. Before she could say anything, I told her, 'Mother, please give me alms'," he wrote.His mother asked him why he had taken to begging and whether there was any shortage at home."I replied, 'Mother, renunciation is my dharma. A yogi's hunger can only be satiated through alms. I have not come here to stay, but to seek alms. Whatever you give me will fulfil my purpose," Adityanath recalled.He said his mother's affection ultimately respected the resolve of her son, who had embraced the monastic life.In the letter, Adityanath also invoked references from Hindu mythology, referring to Mata Kaushalya's blessings when Lord Ram left for exile and Lord Krishna's journey from Mathura's prison to Gokul at his mother's wish."Mother is someone who can take the place of everyone, but no one can take the place of a mother," he wrote.Describing his mother as his first teacher who taught him the basics of education, the chief minister said some debts could never be repaid, though one's duties could certainly be fulfilled.He said he had been striving to fulfil this responsibility towards women and mothers in the state since entering public life.Adityanath appealed to people to pledge their support to destitute mothers, understand the suffering of deprived women and bring smiles to the faces of those in distress.His mother, Savitri Devi, died at her native village in Uttarakhand on Friday morning at the age of 91. The chief minister and his family took her remains from their ancestral home in Panchur village in Pauri Garhwal district on Saturday for the funeral at Chandi Ghat cremation ground in Haridwar.At the ghat, Adityanath looked emotional as he stood by his mother's remains.After paying respect to his mother at their home, Adityanath shared on X, "There is no shade like a mother's, no refuge like a mother's. There is no protection like a mother's, no love like a mother's."

headline: The Bisleri scare: What excess chemicals found by FSSAI do to your body
content: For millions of Indians, buying a bottle of Bisleri is almost instinctive. At railway stations, airports, restaurants and neighbourhood shops, the familiar label has become synonymous with safe drinking water. But a recent action by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has shaken that confidence, raising a larger question: how safe is the bottled water consumers routinely trust? FSSAI has sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd after a regulatory sample of its packaged drinking water was declared unsafe in laboratory examinations. The initial test found that the sample did not meet prescribed limits for bromate. Following an appeal by the company, a referral food laboratory also declared the sample unsafe after detecting polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). Both of these are carcinogens. However, it is important to understand that the findings concern a particular sample. They do not establish that every Bisleri bottle in the market is contaminated, nor do they amount to a judicial conviction. What is bromate? Bromate is an inorganic chemical that can form during water treatment, particularly when ozone is used for disinfection. Ozone destroys harmful microorganisms, but it can react with naturally occurring bromide in source water to produce bromate. This makes careful monitoring of the treatment process essential. The concern is its potential toxicity. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies bromate as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B), based largely on animal studies. Research has associated prolonged exposure with tumours in the kidneys, thyroid and other tissues. Studies have also indicated that bromate can cause oxidative stress and damage DNA. At high exposure levels, bromate poisoning has been associated with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, kidney injury and even hearing impairment. The World Health Organization (WHO) has set a provisional guideline value of 10 micrograms per litre for bromate, reflecting the need to minimise long-term exposure. The second finding, PAHs, is equally concerning. PAHs are a large family of organic chemicals produced mainly through the incomplete burning of materials such as coal, petroleum, wood and other organic matter. They are found in vehicle emissions, industrial pollution, smoke, contaminated soil and certain foods cooked at very high temperatures. Not all PAHs are equally harmful. Benzo[a]pyrene, for instance, is classified by IARC as carcinogenic to humans. Certain PAHs can be metabolised inside the body into compounds that interact with DNA, potentially causing mutations and increasing cancer risk. Research has also examined their possible reproductive, developmental and immune-system effects. The WHO has prescribed a drinking-water guideline of 0.7 micrograms per litre for benzo[a]pyrene. How could such contaminants enter packaged water? The possible routes include contaminated source water, inadequate process controls, environmental pollution and contact with contaminated storage or packaging materials. In the case of bromate, the water-treatment process itself deserves particular scrutiny, especially where ozonation is used. The Bisleri controversy also comes against the backdrop of broader quality-control concerns in India’s packaged-water industry. Government data presented in Parliament in February 2025 showed that of 1,300 enforcement samples of packaged drinking water analysed in 2023–24, 333 were non-conforming. In 2022–23, 650 of 1,776 samples failed to conform to the prescribed standards. What about the regulatory framework? India’s regulatory framework has also undergone a significant change. In October 2024, the government removed the mandatory BIS certification requirement for packaged drinking water and mineral water. This did not free manufacturers from quality-control obligations. FSSAI subsequently introduced a testing scheme for packaged drinking water and mineral water, effective January 1, 2026, to strengthen compliance and monitoring. How can you check bottles? For consumers, the lesson is to look beyond brand familiarity. Check the FSSAI licence details, manufacturer’s address, batch or lot number, packaging date and best-before information before buying. Ensure the cap seal is intact and avoid bottles that are damaged, leaking or visibly contaminated. Buy from retailers who store water away from direct sunlight and excessive heat. But there is a limitation to these precautions: bromate and PAHs cannot reliably be identified through sight, smell or taste. Water that looks perfectly clear can still contain chemical contaminants. Only appropriate laboratory testing can establish their presence. Should consumers stop drinking Bisleri altogether? The available evidence does not justify a blanket conclusion that all its products are unsafe. What it does justify is a demand for transparency. FSSAI should clarify the affected batch, manufacturing facility, actual chemical concentrations and whether further market sampling or a recall is necessary. Bisleri, too, needs to address the findings and make relevant quality-testing information available. Packaged drinking water is often a necessity for Indians who cannot confidently depend on the quality of available drinking supplies. Consumers are entitled to expect that a bottle sold as safe drinking water has undergone rigorous testing and meets prescribed standards.

headline: Pune-Patna Indigo flight diverted to Lucknow due to bad weather
content: An IndiGo flight from Pune to Patna was diverted to Lucknow airport early on Monday due to bad weather in the Bihar capital, airport sources said.Flight 6E 653 landed at Lucknow airport at 2.45 am with 187 passengers, including five infants, and six crew members on board, they said.The flight was expected to resume its journey later on Monday morning, sources said.

headline: Fake cops had him trapped for 11 days. Then a real policeman called
content: On October 1, Bhim Singh was about to liquidate his mutual funds, the last of his savings and the only cushion between a 73-year-old retiree and financial ruin. He had already broken his fixed deposit and sent Rs 25 lakh to men he believed were officers of the law. Now they were scaring him into selling the rest, and he was planning to part with some of his wife’s jewellery. For 11 days, he and his 65-year-old wife had been under “digital arrest” in their modest house in Roshan Pura, a middle-class locality near the Delhi-Gurugram border, confined by people who were never in the room. Then his phone rang again. “Hello, this is Inspector Parveen Kumar, from Delhi Police. Have you transferred the money into this account? Aapke saath scam ho raha hai. Woh police nahi hai (You are being scammed. Those men are not the police),” said the voice on the other end. Singh was in a bind. For days he had been shown an Enforcement Directorate notice, an FIR copy bearing the Supreme Court’s name, and a courtroom where a judge in a black robe presided. Now a stranger was telling him that all of it was false, and that the stranger was the real police. Who was real and who was not had moved beyond his mental grasp. “I initially doubted him,” Singh says. The caller sent him videos of other digital-arrest victims, so that he could see what was happening to him. “I called him and asked if he also wanted to put me under digital arrest. But when he said he did not need money, I was inclined to listen. It was the first time in nearly 15 days that I had not been asked to pay money.” Singh was saved. He did not send another Rs 3.44 lakh he was about to. His rescue was the work of a unit that did not exist in March: the Proactive Victim Identification & Protection Team of the Delhi Police. It is tiny — one inspector and two head constables — and does something Indian policing has rarely tried. “It looks for people in the middle of a digital arrest, while the scam is still running, and tries to talk them out of it,” a senior police official said. Delhi has become one of the country’s most vulnerable cities for digital arrests, and its elderly are the favoured targets. Many live alone while their children work punishing jobs or live abroad. “In digital arrest cases, policing has so far prioritised recovering the money and tracing the accused. But in most cases, once the money moves, it’s gone. It hops across accounts and leaves the formal banking system, through crypto and hawala channels, often before the victim has finished explaining what happened,” says a senior police officer. “Hence, we decided that we should trace the victims and not let the money leave. That’s how the unit was formed in March this year” The special unit If you dial 1930, the national cyber-fraud helpline, from Delhi, the person most likely to pick up is Inspector Kumar. He oversees the helpline’s control room at the Intelligence Fusion and Strategic Operations (IFSO) unit of the Delhi Police. “As I was handling the 1930 helpline, I was the first point of contact for the victims,” he says. “They usually called with such distress, with no idea of what had befallen them. So I had the practice of being extremely patient and sensitive to each caller.” When the police set up the new team in March, they gave it to Kumar to handle. Senior officers say the choice came down to that patience, and to the fact that he already coordinated regularly with both IFSO and the Ministry of Home Affairs’ Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre, or I4C. Kumar works from IFSO’s Rohini branch. His two deputies, the head constables, operate from the cyber agency’s offices at Connaught Place. The mandate, Kumar says, went beyond answering complaints. The team was asked to reach people while they were still being duped, in real time. “We have to save the victim, and anyhow keep them engaged,” he says. “No matter what they say to us, or how difficult they are to convince.” The team’s main operation is to track suspected money transactions, and to find the next victim before the money moves again. “Whenever we get a cyber fraud complaint, we first get the details of the account the victim transferred the money to,” Kumar says. “The head constables at Connaught Place get in touch with the bank, and also get details of the victim. We then check if that (suspect’s) account is still receiving money. If yes, then someone somewhere is still being scammed.” The head constables then try to reach that second victim. But it is not as simple as picking up a phone, says Kumar. Convincing is the hard part, because the police are competing with a well-produced show. The challenge, he says, is that victims believe the scammers are the real police, and the scammers have gone to great lengths to make that belief hold. Victims, he adds, are shown genuine-looking FIRs and official notices, and some sit through live court proceedings. When the head constables cannot get through, Kumar takes over. “It’s difficult to beat that,” says a police officer. “In most of our cases of digital arrest, we call them and tell them that we are the real police. We try to take them into confidence by telling them that we are not going to ask for any money. We send them videos related to cases of digital arrest, so that they can look at it and then realise that the same thing is happening to them.” Once the unit gets through, officers insist that a relative or a friend sits beside the victim for as long as the scammers keep calling. The rescue Similar was the chain of events on September 29, when Bhola Thakur, a 78-year-old retired Army captain from Sagarpur, called 1930. He was emerging from a 15-day “digital arrest” during which he had sent about Rs 4 crore to cyber criminals, in six transactions. “They claimed that SIM cards and credit cards had been issued on his Aadhaar and misused in Canada,” says a police officer. “He was then put on a video call with a person impersonating an IPS officer of PS Daryaganj, who threatened him with arrest in a money laundering case. Out of fear, he transferred a large sum of money in multiple transactions from his BOB, ICICI and SBI accounts.” The police traced where the money went. It had landed in a first-layer mule account at Axis Bank in Hyderabad, Telangana, and the account was still filling. Between September 21 and September 29, another Rs 1.45 crore had poured in from five different accounts. They belonged to a retired Indian Railways employee, 70; a cloth trader, 80, from Rajasthan; a businessman, 50, from Gujarat; a hospital assistant, 65, from Maharashtra; and Bhim Singh. When Inspector Kumar called Singh he was getting ready to send another Rs 3.44 lakh to the men who had kept him under “digital arrest”, and was planning to sell some of his wife’s jewellery. Like Singh, the other four — three of them elderly and each at a different stage of “digital arrest” — were stopped from sending more money. In all, the Delhi Police says, they kept more than Rs 75 lakh out of the fraudsters’ hands. But what had already been sent could not be saved. “The money that had been transferred had already moved to other accounts,” says a police officer. “It is now not in the formal banking system. So, it’s difficult to say how it will be recovered.” The challenges The team now handles two to three digital arrest cases every day. However, multiple officers say that at present, saving a victim of digital arrest is still an exception. One senior officer says that of every 10 calls made to victims, perhaps only one or two end as Singh’s did. Another senior officer said the rate of saving a victim from further loss is closer to one in 15. According to the I4C, at least 21,900 complaints of digital-arrest fraud came in between January and August this year, and more than Rs 647 crore was lost. How much was recovered is not known. At an open-house discussion on safeguarding human rights against digital arrest scams, Justice V Ramasubramanian, chairperson of the National Human Rights Commission, said that recovering even a part of the money was a hassle for victims. The legal and procedural processes, he said, proved lengthy, costly and distressing. “At times, the process of recovery becomes more painful than the process of losing money.” Trust a hurdle Trust is the next hurdle. “Lonely senior citizens are also very sceptical,” says another officer who has worked with IFSO. “After paying that much to fake cops, it’s difficult for them to trust again when they are called by the real ones.” Kumar remembers a case from June, when he found that an account in Gujarat’s Jamnagar had transferred more than Rs 25 lakh to a mule account. “He was a senior citizen and refused to believe me. Even after I asked him to call 1930,” Kumar says. “I then called the local SHO in the area, who visited his house with a team. But the man didn’t open the door. He had told the fraudsters that people dressed in khaki were standing outside. The scammer convinced him that the SHO was a fraud, and the team ended up waiting hours outside his house.” Why scam can’t be stopped at the start? There is also a limit built into the method. The unit can identify a victim only after that person has sent money to the fraudster at least once, so it cannot stop a scam at the start. For middle-class and lower-middle-class families, the first few transactions often take most of their savings. Singh handed over Rs 25 lakh in one go and had only Rs 3-4 lakh left to transfer. Finally, there is the question of scale. The obvious answer would be to spread the work across district cyber police stations, but senior officers say that could cost them the “golden hour.” “It sounds like a good idea. But you have to understand that the first call will always come to us, as we handle the 1930 control room,” says Additional Commissioner of Police (IFSO) Sanjay Bhatia. “The time we will spend alerting the PS, and getting them in touch with the victim, can be used to stop the transaction. Also, the process of finding the victim requires us getting details from the banks. As every major bank’s nodal officer is connected to IFSO, it’s easier for us to access them,” Bhatia adds.

headline: Blurred, Tiny Text In Class 10 NCERT Book: Council Assures Strict Action Against Erring Printers
content: Following the complaint raised by advocate Vineet Jindal over poor printing quality in his son’s Class 10 NCERT textbook, the National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) has taken cognisance of the matter and assured strict action against printers found responsible. Jindal flagged the issue in a post on X, alleging that the text in his son’s textbook was extremely small, blurred and poorly printed, making it difficult for students to read comfortably. He also raised concerns that prolonged reading of textbooks with such printing defects could lead to eye strain, headaches and other health-related problems among schoolchildren. In his post, Jindal urged Union Education Minister Pralhad Joshi, the Ministry of Education and NCERT to take immediate cognisance of the issue, review printing standards and ensure that students receive clear, readable and student-friendly textbooks. My son is in Class X, and after going through his NCERT textbook, I am deeply concerned about the quality of printing. The text is extremely small, blurred and poorly printed, making it difficult for students to read comfortably. NCERT must understand that such poor-quality textbooks can cause unnecessary eye strain, headaches and other health concerns among schoolchildren. Education should empower young minds, not compromise their health. I urge @JoshiPralhad @EduMinOfIndia and @ncert to take immediate cognisance of this issue, review the printing standards and ensure that students receive clear, readable and student-friendly textbooks. — Adv.Vineet Jindal Office (@VineetJindal_) November 22, 2026 Jindal further added that the concerns extend beyond blurred or double-printed text to include font size, print quality, clarity and the overall readability of NCERT Class 10 textbooks. “The issue is not limited to blurred or double-printed text. The font size, printing quality, clarity and overall readability of NCERT Class X textbooks are equally serious concerns. I wonder whether even NCERT officials would find it comfortable to read such small fonts for extended periods. Poor-quality printing and small fonts can cause unnecessary eye strain and make learning difficult for students,” he commented on the post. Responding to the complaint, NCERT said it was taking the matter seriously and examining it on priority. “Strict action will be initiated against any printer found responsible,” the council said in its post on X, reiterating its commitment to providing clear, readable and student-friendly textbooks for every child. NCERT has taken cognisance of the print-quality concern, is viewing it seriously and is examining it on priority. Strict action will be initiated against any printer found responsible. NCERT remains committed to providing clear, readable, student-friendly textbooks for every child. — NCERT (@ncert) November 22, 2026 The complaint has brought attention to the importance of quality checks in the printing and distribution of school textbooks, particularly those used by students preparing for the Class 10 board examinations.

headline: US ports facing growing wave of cyberattack attempts targeting vital infrastructure: Report | Hindustan Times
content: US ports are facing a growing wave of cyberattacks, with hackers attempting to break into systems that support shipping, trade and energy exports. The attacks are becoming more frequent and sophisticated, while advances in artificial intelligence could help hackers find weaknesses faster.The Port of Corpus Christi in Texas is the biggest US gateway for crude oil exports, shipping around 2.3 million barrels a day, according to the Financial Times. Its chief executive, Kent Britton, said attacks have surged to "hundreds if not thousands" each day. He said they come from “known bad actor” countries and groups looking for high-profile targets, but he did not name any attackers.Hackers are searching the port's computer systems for weak spots. They are also sending fake messages that look like they come from senior executives, to trick staff into giving them access. "They're poking at our systems and trying to find vulnerabilities," Britton said. “With AI, it'll only get more complicated.”Britton said the port is asking Washington for more help. "If you're playing defense, you have to get it right every time," he said. “If you're planning offence, you only have to get it right once,” as per the Financial Times.Also read: Trump blames Democrats midterms victory for stock market wipeout, claims he predicted itOther ports and ships under attackThe Port of Los Angeles, the country's busiest port, said it stopped 120 million attempted attacks in August. The attacks are also hitting ships and shipping firms, according to the Financial Times. The US Coast Guard reported a 17% rise in cyber incidents at sea last year. Two US-bound oil tankers carrying crude oil and liquefied petroleum gas were hacked near the Strait of Gibraltar, and the Coast Guard and FBI boarded them on August 21 and 24 to check their systems. No suspects have been named.North Carolina Ports said in August that an "outside actor" attacked its IT systems. The attack was contained a day later, but gate openings were delayed and the port had to switch to manual work. Shipping giant Maersk also reported that hackers stole data in a recent break-in, but said its operations were not affected and that it was not a ransomware attack.Also read: IDF’s intelligence officials warned Netanyahu against unilateral Israeli attack on Iran: ReportThe Financial Times said experts link countries such as Iran, North Korea and China to hacking aimed at shipping, though groups often route their work through other countries. The FBI recently warned that hackers are using an AI tool called Artex to automate attacks.The Port of Virginia said the threat is now "more acute because of the rise of AI," according to the Financial Times. It said it has not yet suffered a successful breach, but spokesperson Joe Harris warned of serious results. "We're an economic pinch point," he said. “Getting taken offline is not an option.”

headline: 8th Pay Commission: Check how ₹25,000, ₹35,000 and ₹50,000 basic salaries could change under proposed fitment factors
content: Central government employees, pensioners and associated stakeholders are eagerly awaiting the 8th Pay Commission recommendations, as the 7th Pay Commission's 10-year term ended on 31 December 2025. There is anticipation of significant revisions to the basic salaries of central government employees, depending on the fitment factor. Several prominent employee unions have proposed different multipliers for consideration by the 8th Pay Commission. The multipliers put forward by unions are based on inflation expectations. Assuming these fitment factors are accepted by the 8th Pay Commission and implemented by the central government, here is how the basic pay of central government employees could change if their basic pay is ₹25,000, ₹35,000 or ₹50,000. The fitment factor is a multiplier used to calculate the ‘revised basic pay’ under the Pay Commission.

headline: No Israeli Government In Sight? Netanyahu, Eisenkot Fail To Break Deadlock After Four-Hour Talks
content: Israeli caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud Party and Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar Party failed to reach an agreement on forming a potential coalition government following their latest round of negotiations, leaving the country’s political deadlock unresolved. The two parties held a four-hour meeting at a hotel in Herzliya, near Tel Aviv, following their first round of discussions last Sunday. In a joint statement, the parties said they had discussed their positions on several key issues but had yet to reach a breakthrough. “The latest round of coalition talks… has concluded. The two sides outlined their positions on a range of substantive issues and discussed them in detail,” the statement said. The parties added that another meeting would take place, although they did not announce a date or provide further details. Eisenkot Faces December 6 Deadline To Form Government Eisenkot faces a December 6 deadline to assemble a governing coalition, with the possibility of seeking an additional two weeks. The October election left neither side with enough parliamentary seats to form a government independently, complicating efforts to secure a majority. Eisenkot’s faction holds 48 seats, short of the 61 required for a parliamentary majority. Internal disagreements over potential coalition partners have further complicated negotiations. Options under consideration include bringing ultra-Orthodox parties into the coalition, securing support from Arab parties or exploring a power-sharing arrangement with Likud. Netanyahu Pushes For Power-Sharing Deal Netanyahu is advocating a national unity government that could involve sharing the premiership with Eisenkot through a rotational arrangement, a model Israel has used in the past. Such an arrangement could help Netanyahu retain political safeguards amid the corruption allegations he faces. However, the proposal faces resistance from Eisenkot, who ruled out joining a government headed by Netanyahu. Eisenkot’s ally and former prime minister Naftali Bennett also reiterated that he would not join any coalition involving “Netanyahu or his bloc, under any circumstances”.

headline: US seeks India partnership on Dalai Lama succession, warns of China's influence
content: The bipartisan commission wants Washington to recognise the Gaden Phodrang Trust as the sole authority to identify the Dalai Lama's successor and reject any candidate selected by Beijing !Image 1: File photo: ibetan Spiritual leader the Dalai Lama during an event organised as part of his 90th Birthday celebrations, at the Tsuglagkhang temple, McLeodganj, in Kangra district, Himachal Pradesh, Saturday, Sept. 20, 2025. File photo: ibetan Spiritual leader the Dalai Lama during an event organised as part of his 90th Birthday celebrations, at the Tsuglagkhang temple, McLeodganj, in Kangra district, Himachal Pradesh, Saturday, Sept. 20, 2025. PTI A US Congressional panel has recommended setting up of a senior-level channel with India for succession contingency planning to the 14th Dalai Lama, contending that China may turn the process into an international contest over legitimacy. The US-China Economic and Security Review Commission, in a report to the US Congress, made a strong pitch to recognise the Gaden Phodrang Trust as the sole legitimate authority to identify and recognise the successor to the 14th Dalai Lama.

headline: Patiala school marks 125 years of CFMSS mission in India
content: The highlight of the evening was a magnificent theatrical presentation depicting the visionary mission of Venerable Mother Seraphina Farolfi and the four pioneering Sisters who arrived in India in 1901. Through evocative enactments, music and choreography, students brought alive their arduous journey, pioneering contribution to girls’ education and compassionate humanitarian service during the Partition.The jubilant portrayal of India’s Independence stirred patriotic fervour, while the poignant depiction of Partition, particularly the tragic Partition-era train journeys, left many spectators visibly moved, with moist eyes. The presentation poignantly highlighted the Sisters’ unwavering commitment to peace, humanity and compassionate service, transcending religious and geographical boundaries even amidst immense human suffering.A vibrant cultural extravaganza celebrating India’s rich heritage enthralled the audience. Class X board examination achievers of 2025–26 were also felicitated.The celebration reaffirmed that the light kindled by Mother Seraphina continues to illuminate generations through education, compassion and selfless service.Our Lady of Fatima Convent Secondary School, Patiala, celebrated its annual function on the theme, “Light Across the Seas: 125 Years of CFMSS Mission in India,” commemorating the congregation’s legacy of faith, education and selfless service.Chief guest Ankita Kansal, Assistant Commissioner, Mohali, and guest of honour Sumeet Sharma, Associate Vice-President, Wipro, both alumni of the school, attended the event. A theatrical presentation highlighted the mission of Venerable Mother Seraphina Farolfi and the four Sisters who arrived in India in 1901, showcasing their contribution to girls’ education and humanitarian service. Class X board examination achievers of 2025-26 were felicitated on the occasion.

headline: UK government to make case for greater public control of utilities | Hindustan Times
content: LONDON, - Britain's Labour government will set out details of why it wants more public control of energy and water utilities on Monday when senior minister Louise Haigh addresses the annual conference of lobby group the Confederation of British Industry.Prime Minister Andy Burnham has blamed privatisation of utilities in the 1980s and 1990s, followed by poor regulation, for excess profits, high energy prices and the failure of some water companies to stop releasing sewage into rivers and the sea.According to Haigh's office, she will tell the CBI that the government wants a new partnership with private capital, "built on clear rules, clear expectations and a fair return on investment".* Haigh will say the government does not want "wholesale nationalisation" of utilities, but is concerned that effective monopolies have led to a lack of genuine competition * Haigh will also highlight that Britain's utilities sector is an outlier in enabling foreign governments to own significant stakes* Burnham set out plans in September to reverse legislation that bars the government from owning more than 3% of water utilities in England and is expected to give more details on utility regulation next month* CBI Chief Executive Rain Newton-Smith said she wanted reassurance that greater public control was consistent with "private capital at the table... not heading for the exit", and would not create undue fears of renationalisation* Thames Water – which supplies 16 million customers in and around London – has been regarded as at risk of a costly renationalisation and is restructuring its £20 billion of debt after mounting fines for pollution* In a statement responding to Labour's plans for British utilities, Conservative Party finance spokesperson Andrew Griffith said nationalisation would not lower bills and the government should put less focus on achieving net zero* Also at the CBI conference, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage plans to criticise big businesses for backing closer EU ties, which he said would raise regulatory costs for their smaller competitors and let them hire cheaper EU workers instead of BritonsThis article was generated from an automated news agency feed without modifications to text.
